Mr. A10NK. I explained when introducing this Bill that its object was to correct a clerical error in the Revised Statutes of Canada. Mr. AlONK. This resolution is presented to -the House under the fallowing circumstances :
On November 9, 1909, application was made by the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company, Limited, for a subsidy, under the Act of 1908, to encourage the construction of dry docks, and specification and plans were submitted for a dock of the

While the plans, specification and estimates for this dock were under consideration by the department, with the object of arriving at the total sum upon which subsidy should he granted, the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, chap. 24, of the Statutes of 1908, was repealed by chap. 17 of the Statutes of 1910, which was assented to on the 4th of Alay, 1910. A recommendation was sent to

*council on the 4th May, and an order in -council passed on the 11th May, 1910, authorizing the department to enter into an agreement with the Co'llingwood Shipbuilding Company, Limited, to grant a subsidy -on Dry Dock No, 2, of 3 per cent on $306,365.18, for twenty years. The Dry Docks Subsidies Act, chap. 17, of the Statutes of 1910, provides for the payment of subsidy on three different classes of docks, of which the third class is limited to a cost of not more than $1,500,000 with a subsidy of 3 per cent for twenty years. A third class dock must be 400 feet in length, 65 feet wide and 18 feet over the sill at ordinary low water when constructed in non-tidal waters. The Collingwood Dry Dock No. 2 possessed the necessary length and width, but was only 16 feet on the sill at low water, so that it did not qualify under the new legislation. As, however, the consideration of this application, made under the 1908 Act, had been completed before the passing of the Act of 1910, containing the new conditions, and as the dock was, in addition, at that time partially constructed, it was considered only fair that the dock should be subsidized and that special legislation should be introduced -at the next session of parliament to enable payment of the subsidy. Accordingly, on the 17th May, 1911, a resolution was moved by the honourable the Minister of Public Works, ns follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to ratify and [DOT]confirm an agreement between the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company, Limited, and His Majesty, dated the 27th day of July, 1910, respecting the construction of a dry dock at the town of Collingwood, and to authorize the Governor in Council to pay an annual subsidy of three per cent, per annum for 20 years upon the sum of $306,965.18 being the cost of the construction of the dry dock, &c.
A draft Bill was also prepared, but was never introduced; the resolution still remaining on the order paper when parliament dissolved.
Under these circumstances the department is submitting the same resolution to the House. I do not think there is any doubt that the company is entitled to The subsidy under the circumstances.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.

House in Committee on Bill (No. 32) respecting Grain.-Mr. Foster (North Toronto).
On section 96-regulations as to binning and cleaning

I wish to add a clause as subsection 2 of which I gave notice. This, I think, should be changed in the latter half, after the words ' any terminal warehouseman neglecting to comply within thirty days.' That seems a long time to give, and it might be well to strike out the words ' within thirty days ' and insert the words ' within a reasonable time.' Thirty days seems altogether too long, and in some cases would be. In other cases thirty days might be too short if the improvements to be made involve a good deal of altering and changing. I do not see any better way of arranging it, except to say within reasonable time.

I would suggest that it be made: 'within reasonable time not exceeding thirty days ' because in the rush of the grain season, unless the alteration can be made within thirty days there is no use making it at all.
I am quite willing to put that in. Then we will insert the word ' comply ', ' within reasonable time not exceeding thirty days '. I move the adoption of the clause as amended.
The term used in the ' Hansard ' report of the previous debate is ' punishable ' not ' liable
The law clerk put in the other word as being a better legal term.
Before the minister leaves that page may I ask if he has come to any decision in regard to overages which is alluded to in subsection 7 of section 95?

The whole matter is under consideration. The overages for 1909-10 were considerable- more than considerable in fact. In 1910-11 the overages and shortages showed over the whole quantity of wheat which was passed through, probably 90,000,000 or 100,000,000, a balance of only about 35,000 bushels which is an almost infinitesimal percentage on the whole amount carried through. I am having the whole subject looked into now in view of establishing a basis as to what shall be done as between the shortages and overages. Of course we have a claim upon the elevator men for shortages, but they argue that if they make up the shortages they ought to be entitled to the overages. It is a perfectly allowable claim, I think that they should be entitled to the overages up to the amount that will balance the shortages. Over and above that there may be a question, but I am looking into the subject with my officers so as to come to a basis upon which this shall be regulated.

If you allow the elevators overages up to what would be a reasonable allowance for legitimate error in weighing, I think they could have no claim or right for anything over and above that, no matter what is done in regard to the shortages.
Section as amended agreed to.
Has the minister anything to inform the committee as to the effect of certificates on grain which passes through the States?

I am also taking that matter up with various officers of our own, and of the United States Chambers of Commerce in the different ports. I am getting complete information as to what the custom is all the way through from the time the grain leaves our border until it takes a ship either at New York, Boston or Portland or at any of our own ports.
There will be no result from that investigation so far as the Act is concerned?

No. It will be a guidance for the future.
On section 104-offices in Winnipeg,

The next is section 104. I gave notice of that, and moved that a section follow to be denominated 104A. That section is to be found in ' Hansard.' It provides for an official Survey Board to be established for the district of Calgary in the western inspection division-for the manner in which that Survey Board shall be selected-and then applies the positions of other sections applicable thereto. The question raisedi the other day was a3 to wtietner it was wiser to allow the Survey Board to be appointed ultimately by the board upon competent persons being selected by the Board of Trade of Calgary. 1 think the hon. gentleman who raised the point favoured something like the plan that exists in the Survey Board towards the eastern end of the western inspection division. As I said then, that has worked out in practice to leave the work of the Survey Board completely with the members of it which were nominated by the Board of Trade of Winnipeg. The others having other business to attend to, and not being upon the grain exchange, find it inconvenient to attend and do not attend. In Calgary if you place two nominees from Manitoba, two from Saskatchewan and two from Alberta, the same thing would probably happen, and it would seem that if the board had the competency of the Survey Board within their own hands, there should be no difficulty in getting men eligible in Calgary, on the nomination of the Board
of Trade, who would be perfectly fitted to act. There would be no objection, if it were thought best, to have the Minister of Agriculture of Alberta make the nomination. But even then, I think, it should be a person resident in Calgary. And, if it were not so nominated in the Bill, it seems to me you would have a supernumerary rather than a helpful member of the board. I think we should get all that is necessary, and in thoroughly workable foTm under the plan I have intimated here. I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has any fixed convictions on this subject or not.

I have taken some interest in this provision since my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) brought it in the other day. Conditions in Calgary are different from those in Winnipeg. In Winnipeg, the grain trade interests a very large proportion of the business community, whereas the grain trade does not interest a large proportion of the business community in Calgary. Besides, Calgary, of course, is a much smaller place than Winnipeg. Therefore, we could not look for absolutely the same conditions surrounding the appointment of members of the Survey Board on the nomination of the Board of Trade of Calgary as in the case of those nominated by the Board of Trade of Winnipeg. For these reasons, I could think it desirable that the provincial governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan should have the authority to make nominations. I include Saskatchewan because it is expected that some Saskatchewan grain as well as Alberta grain will go through Calgary. I appreciate the desirability of the appointees being residents of Calgary; but I think that, perhaps, it might be wise not to require that by the terms of the Act. What I should like would be that the government of Alberta and the government of Saskatchewan should have the right to appoint two members each. It might be left to their good judgment whether they would appoint residents of Calgary or not. I have had discussion with parties well informed upon, and interested in, this matter, and they consider that six is not a sufficiently large board for Calgary. Under the provisions of the law no person is allowed to sit on a survey who is interested in the transaction under survey. With the small number of people interested in the grain trade in Calgary, and with a small board, it might be difficult to get a Survey Board in a position to act. Too many of the members of the small board might be interested in its transactions and, therefore, incapacitated from sitting. While it might seem that the large board is more cumbersome, it is not necessarily

more cumbersome. On the contrary, it may be more workable and more available for work, provided the members are conveniently resident in the city where the transaction under survey takes place.

I quite see the point that my non. friend (Mr. Oliver) makes. Part of it has weight, but he will excuse me if I say that the other has not quite so much weight. Calgary is not at present a grain centre such as Winnipeg, and it may be some little time before Calgary attains any such position. But all the aspirations and all the prospects with reference to the matter point to the belief that Calgary will, before very long, become a very important grain centre. And there will not be very much work to do until it has grown in importance, and it is very likely to grow in importance very quickly, depending upon the exits for grain which are available. It seems to me it would not be difficult to find in Calgary, where they have a population of
50,000	a large proportion of whom are business men, the material for a board of six. There is something, however, I think, in what my hon. friend says about responsibility. If one is appointed by the provincial government he is rather amenable to the responsible authority of that province. And if we include Alberta, Saskatchewan also should be included. There is no reason to include Manitoba, because Manitoba grain will probably not seek a market by way of the west. We must be sure to provide that a quorum is to be had, and non-resident members are a difficulty in that respect. If one happens to bo interested in the transaction and, therefore, ineligible, and if there are two or three or four non-residents, the making of a quorum may be difficult-. Perhaps it would answer if we make the board a board of eight and provide that the provincial government of Alberta and the provincial government of Saskatchewan shall each nominate one.
I should much prefer to have it two from each provincial government, but I would certainly rather have one than none.
Considr ering the number of the whole Survey Board, I should think that one from each province would be enough. I move the amendment of this section.
Has the minister thought that in Calgary it may be difficult to find six people who are experienced in regard to the duties which will be put upon them under this Act?

I have not thought so. If that were the condition, I should think it premature to erect Mr. OLIVER.
a Survey Board there at all. They must have the six experts, but if they can find no people except those who are incompetent, those people will not be approved of, and so there will not be a Survey Board.

I would not think that that was evidence of this being premature, because it is the interest of the grain trade which is dominant, and not- that of the citizens of Calgary. The province of Alberta, with all due respect for it, is not a grain growing province such as Saskatchewan or Manitoba. Of course, it excels in other things, in which they do not excel. In line with what the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has said, and in addition to what I have said, we are to remember that the people of Calgary have not been trained in that kind of business. It is easy, of course, to criticise, but unquestionably it is more or less owing to the experiment of preparing for what we hope will be a great movement of our grain westward. I certainly do not wish to throw any obstacles in the way of that movement, but I doubt that you will find men who will sufficiently excel in the knowledge of the .grain business to be appointed to this board.
I stand up for Calgary in that respect; I think there is enough both of ability and experience to be found in that city for the creation of this board.
There is not an elevator in the place except those connected with the mill.

They might not be good judges of elevators but they might be good judges of grain, and that is what they are there for. I think my hon. friend's fears are leading away his judgment.
On section 115.

1 gave notice of a new section to be substituted for this one:
All good grain that has an excessive moisture, being tough, damp or wet or otherwise unfit for warehousing, shall be entered on the inspecting officer's book as ' no grade ' with his notations as to quality and condition.
All grain that is unsound, musty, dirty, smutty, sprouted or contains a large admixture of other kinds of grain, seeds or wild oats, or from any other cause is unfit to be classed under any of the recognized grades, shall be classed as ' rejected,' with the inspector's notations as to quality and condition.

There is a very radical change from the old clause, and I am not quite clear as to the reasons for the change, that is, good mixed grain, or mixed grain of good quality, is changed from low grade to rejected. I would like to know on what ground that change is made.

The reason for the change is two-fold. In the first place, the custom has been all along to grade the grain, and it has so been known and graded as is set forth in the substituted section. The first has reference entirely to moisture, that is the prime element in it..

That kind of grain is
brought into the rejected class.
It was left out of the first class, and is put into the class of rejected.
On the face of it, it strikes me that the change is hardly justified. I am not an expert in grain, but I would like to know the reason why the change has been made.

It has always been graded that way, that is the general grade all the way through, and it is belter to have the law put in consonance with the practice. But I believe the contention is that the practice is the correct way.
On section 125: security by license,

That has reference to the bond. We had some conversation about it. I have given it considerable thought, and I propose to amend it in this way:	The clause, as it reads,
provides for a penal sum of not less than $10,000, and .not more than $50,000. These are two arbitrary sums. There does not seem to be any orinciple which underlies the fixing of these sums. If you have a small elevator of 25,000 or 30,000 bushels, although I believe the smallest at Fort William at the present time, is about 65,000 bushels, you can tax it $10,000 and if you have one of 7,000,000 bushels capacity you cannot have the bond larger than $50,000. That appears to be unfair, and I have been making some inquiry about it. I think it is undeniable that the bond imposed upon these terminal elevators, which have very responsible duties thrown upon them and are restricted by very close laws and regulations, the strictness of which has been conditioned by the necessity of preventing violations, should be adequate to the restrictions and responsibilities. In the state of Minnesota I find that they have a bond proportioned to the capacity of the elevator and, on inquiry, I also find that the country elevator system in Canada is run at the present time, where bonds are required, upon that principle. The bond is proportioned to the capacity of the elevator and in so far as I can learn, the system has worked well. So, I propose to apply the same principle to the terminal elevators. But, I do not seem to have the amendment in the form in which I arranged it, and therefore, we will let this section stand in the meantime.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 126, subsection 8: grades not to be mixed,

The section as at present reads:
In no case, whether in a terminal elevator in the western inspection division or in a public elevator in the eastern inspection division, shall grain of different grades be mixed together while in store.
I propose to add the words ' or public ' after 'terminal,' so that it will read:
In no case, whether in a terminal or public elevator.. . . shall grain of different grades be mixed together while in store.
I think that covers the whole question.
That is all right.
What is a public elevator?
A public elevator is an elevator in which grain, in inspected in, stored and inspected out again.	-
What is a terminal elevator?

A public elevator may not be a terminal elevator. A terminal elevator must be at a terminal point, whereas a public elevator may be outside of a terminal point. Is my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) satisfied with this?

Yes.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 132: no limiting of liability of warehouseman,

The section reads:
No terminal warehouseman shall insert in any receipt issued by him any language in any wise limiting or modifying his liabilities or responsibility, except as in this part mentioned and except in so far as all parties concerned consent thereto.
I have on examination concluded that it is not right to leave these words in, and I propose to strike out all words after ' mentioned.' The warehouse receipt is_ a very important document, it embodies contracts and if you allow a plea to be put up that so and so has agreed to have it otherwise, it will lead to interminable confusion.
On section 151a,

I Dro-pose to add to 151 a subsection providing that seed elevators shall not be obliged to store grain for outsiders. It permits.

them to do so but does not compel them. While thus protecting the operators of seed elevators, we require them to be licensed and to come under supervision.
On section 159,

It was proposed to add a subsection to subsection 4, which provided that the owner of the grain shall have an absolute right of direction of the shipment of that grain for 48 hours after he has placed it in the elevator. On consideration I have decided that this amendment, which was proposed by the hon. member for Moose)aw (Mr. Knowles), does not give to the owner of the grain any right which he does not now possess under subsection 4.

I was not present at the last discussion of this section. I quite realize the necessity of the section, but it is a most arbitrary provision and an arbitrary provision in any law is liable to abuse and abuses have arisen. I am inclined to think that the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Moosejaw would establish a principle that would be of some substantial advantage to the owner of the grain.

I am not a lawyer, but it strikes me in looking at the English of the section that the proposed subsection gives no more right of detention of the grain than is given under subsection 4. So far as I am concerned, I have no objection to providing for 48 hours of absolute detention if the committee think it best, so as to give an opportunity to the shipper of the grain to change his mind and send it somewhere else if he can make a better sale; but this would not very often happen, as we find by experience.

The implication in the section seems to be that the elevator man, being subject to the requirement, would be prevented from shipping the grain before forty-eight hours had elapsed. The principle, I think, is sufficiently important to warrant us in recognizing the proprietary rights of the owner of the grain for a short period after he puts his grain into the elevator, so that the elevator man shall not be at liberty to ship it out say an hour after he receives it. This point is perhaps more important In Alberta than in Manitoba or Saskatchewan, owing to the possibility of grain from Alberta being routed east or west. It is for that reason that I am somewhat stronger on the point than my hon. friend perhaps thinks I should be.

I will make an amendment which will make it obligatory on the elevator man to allow Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
forty-eight hours to pass before the shipment is made. The farmer, of course, can waive that at any time.
If it is made obligatory on the elevator man to give forty-eight hours' notice before the grain goes out,_ this provides- all the protection that is given absolutely by subsection 4 of section 159.
If section 164 is passed as amended, it accomplishes everything that is necessary.

I would call the minister's attention to the fact that his amendment in section 164 does not provide for the shipper waiving his right so that the grain could be sent off the very day it was put in if he wanted that done.

I will see that the waiver is put into section 164 in the same wray that it is in section 159.
On section 169-special bins,
I propose to strike out the words ' to any buyer ' which should not be in there.
I think there is a mix up about this section that perhaps is not covered by the amendment my hon. friend proposes unless he has some other amendment.

I have given some attention to the section and it strikes me as being all right. The special bin in a flat warehouse is only granted to farmers?
Mr. FOSTER	(North Toronto).	That
is all.
I am sure it is not intended to restrict a bin in a country elevator to farmers?

No it is not.
(Mr. OLIVER. Yet that is what this section would do as amended. On section 191-dimensions of loading platforms.

This takes up the question of the loading platform which I promised to look into, to see if anything could be done to reconcile the warring factions. I now propose to insert the following after the word ' Board ' in the 26th line, ' which shall be of such height, width and length as the board prescribes, provided that in no case shall the length exceed 100 feet nor the width 24 feet.

On section 207, special powers to board to order supply of cars,

It is proposed to substitute for section 207 the section of which I gave notice, and which, I believe, has been printed. This amended section provides for all the cases of discretion permitted to the warehouse men, and now to the board under the Manitoba Grain Act, which is found in ' A ' elevators that are in danger of collapse and in ' D ' where there is a liability to heating, and also for the other two cases which were placed in Bill 96 which we passed in this House, which was passed also in the Senate, and is now in operation. It adds also subsection 'E' as follows:
(e) Whenever, after due examination, the board considers it necessary and advisable in order to relieve congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain.
I do not know that it is necessary to explain, after the discussions' we have'had upon the clause in the Bill which has become law, why this subsection (e) is added here. It would seem proper that the board, which has the whole range of the grain transport in its eye and under its management, should have this discretion vested in it. When, in any particular case it is represented that there is congestion, or the despatch of gram is hindered, the board may make due investigation, and if, after due consideration, it deems it necessary and advisaole to relieve the congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain, it is given discretion and power to so order. The purpose is fully explained by the subsection itself. With
reference to this matter many objections and representations have been made. One petition has been received from the Credit Men's Association or Business Men's Association, petitions which have been largely signed and numerous copies of which and signatures to which have come into the office, asking for the suspension of the car order provision. Now, the suspension of the car order provision is a very different thing from the granting of this discretionary power to the Board of Grain Commissioners, an extension of the discretionary powers which they, in the person of the Warehouse Commissioner, already have, and which we have extended by our legislation of a few days ago. The moment petitions were circulated and signed in favour of suspending the car order section of the Manitoba Grain Act the farmers and the shippers of grain, of course, were alarmed. They were in complete hostility to the suspension of the car order provisions, for they remembered the situation some years ago, and which was relieved for them by the enactments made in 1905. And they were properly apprehensive of having the provisions suspended or done away with even temporarily, for fear that the old conditions might be brought back.
Now on that apprehension, and with that view, numerous letters and petitions have been forwarded to the department 'praying that the car order provisions of the Manitoba Grain Act be not disturbed. These two different petitions have come in and have been considered. I made some remarks in reference to this the other day. Whilst there are very strong representations made that it would be more economical and more in accordance with the general purposes and operations of the railway companies in their transport system, to give them the fullest privilege and powers over the distribution of their cars; on the other hand the situation in the west is a peculiar situation. We do not propose for a moment to interfere with the present security of the farmer gained for him by that legislation. At the same time, conditions are various in the northwest, and changes take place from season to season; and with all due regard for those rights and their preservation, I think we will not make a mistake if we give to the Board of Grain Commissioners the restricted but added discretion that is provided for in subsection (e). If you examine the car order provisions and also the practical working out of the same, you can see they are not based on grounds of absolute equality of privilege. The provisions are such that every man who has half a carload *of grain to ship, in conjunction with his neighbour who may have half a carload of grain to ship, has the. privilege of call-

ing for one car, and for one car only until all other orders are tilled. The large farmer who has many thousands of bushels of grain just as valuable to him in its way as the smaller crop is to the smaller farmer, has the privilege of calling for and placing on the order book one car, and until all orders are filled he gets no other. The elevator which is patronized by the buyer, and by the farmer as well to a very large extent, and which serves as both store house and forwarder for the farmers' grain, though it may contain 25,000 bushels or 100,000 bushels, has the privilege of calling for but one car on the order book, and until his turn comes again he gets no more as an elevator company or as an elevator man. The same is carried out all the way through. It is not, then as I say, based on grounds of equality of interest. I am not here to argue that it ought to be altogether based on the grounds of equality of interest in grain to be shipped; for I think if there is any one who needs to be protected, any one who needs to be cared for especially, even to the placing of restrictions upon others, it is the far distant and isolated and small farmer, who is often but a late comer into the northwest, who comes with his hands, and his team, and has little of this world's goods, who may need advances to be made to him to buy the utensils and stock with which to work, who has often to ask the country storekeeper for sufficient provisions and supplies to keep him until his grain crop matures and can be sold.
That person, I think, not only has a right to our sympathy, but he has a right to all the protection that we can possibly give him consistent with the fair rights of others. I do not need to go into an elaborate discussion of this matter to show to this committee that these rights of the small farmer are not only his best possession,, are not only the ground for his privilege of ordering >a car if he has a carload, but that they are also preserved to him by the facility with which he can get storage and sale of his grain, when it is impossible for him to get a car. I have read a good deal in the newspapers, arid I have stacks of letters in my department which show the difficulties, and troubles, and the almost absolute necessities of many of the class of people to whom I refer, when after the summer's toil, and the autumn's reaping and the late harvest and threshing of grain, they are able- at last to bring their wagon loads, or their half-wagon loads, of grain to the country station, to find that they cannot get a car, to find that the whole elevator capacity is filled, and that there is no purchaser for their grain because the purchaser has neither car to take away the grain nor elevator in which to store it. Then again, we have the conditions that Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto.)
arise with regard to some sections of the country as to frosting, as to late harvest, as to the dampness which ensues, and the like of that. These are cases when those who have the direction of affairs should specially strive to relieve those persons and those sections of the overplus of their grain when it can be best saved, and often when it must be quickly saved in, order to 'prevent it from being a total loss. We propose to have a Grain Commission which shall be able, efficient, honest and broad-nrnded, and to that Grain Commission I am going-to ask this committee to give the discretions which are provided in this clause.

This is a very important amendment which my hen. friend proposes; it involves a very important principle, and is entitled to the serious consideration of the committee. The legislation contained in this particular part of the Grain Act is, it may be said, very remarkable legislation. It undertakes to deal with the property of one man in the interest of some other man. It is the extreme of what might be called socialistic legislation,; I think, perhaps, the most extreme example of socialistic legislation that is on the statute book of any country. It is for the protection of the individual against corporations, or an aggregate of corporations.
It need not be supposed for a moment that such remarkable legislation would ever have appeared upon the statute-books, or having appeared, would have remained there, had there not been the very strongest reasons why, in the public interest, that legislation should be maintained. It has been on the statute-book for a number of years, it has been bitterly opposed from the very beginning on one side and determinedly supported on the other. There is no possibility of the two parties to this, what might be called, irrepressible conflict, coming to any amicable agreement. There is only one thing to do, and 'that is to take sides with one party or the other, either to maintain the position which has been maintained in the legislation that is now on the statute-book and stand for the right of the individual, or give up that legislation and permit the corporation to have its way. I have heard what my hon. friend has said with regard to the propriety of giving full authority to the Board of Grain Commissioners. On the same principle that my hon. friend has stated to the House it would be just as right to say that we only need one clause in this Act, namely, to give the Board of Grain Commissioners full authority to manage the grain trade of Canada. We are not going to do that and my hon. friend is not proposing to do it. Within the compass of a very long and complicated Act, an Act of very remarkable detail, he is laying down what shall be done in this, that and the

ether circumstances and conditions. I will admit that this is a remarkable case, but the very fact that this legislation is remarkable is the very reason why the authority of this statute should be there to protect the right of the individual as the only means whereby his right can be efficiently protected and the only means by which he can have confidence in the protection of that right. It, of course, goes without saying that where it is attempted by legislation to interfere with the rights cl property in such a remarkable manner as this Act does interfere with the rights of property and the course of trade and transportation, there can be no question but that there will be inequalities and, if you like, cases of injustice under its provisions. Many individual cases have occurred, and are occurring to-day in which it would have been much better if this Act had not been on the statute-book and transportation companies and grain dealers had their full liberty to transact their business as they might see fit. In many cases it would have been to the interest of the individual grain producer that that condition should have prevailed. That must be admitted and we cannot expect ever to have legislation of this detailed character that will not result in that way. At the same time from every part of the prairie country where people are raising grain there comes the same protest to-day as that which has come on every previous occasion against the abrogation of this, what they consider, safeguard of their right to a share in car distribution not according to the quantity of the grain, but according to priority of demand. I understand that during this present year, unaer the extraordinary circumstances, that have prevailed, there have been occasions when the warehouse commissioner lias gone outside of the terms of the Act, and, in defiance of the Act, has ordered cars to certain places for the purpose of relieving the extraordinary conditions that prevailed there at the time. 1 am quite aware that the provision which my hon. friend proposes to insert in the Act, merely places, by authority of statute in the hands of the board, which is to be appointed, the right to do what has been done, under these urgent conditions without the sanction of law. I hold the view that although there is that precedent for this provision of the Act, it is still in the interest of the people who are the most intimately concerned that the Act should remain as it is. Even if relief, such as has been given during the past year, cannot be granted if the Act remains as it is, still the mind of the people of the west is that the Act should remain as it is and that there should not be that possibility of variation in its terms that my hon. friend suggests. There is a provision for
variation in this section. It provides that in the case of an elevator in danger of collapsing or in the case of the grain in the elevator being in danger of heating, they shall have a right to a special order of cars. It would be quite right to add a provision as to a special order of cars in the case of distributing seed grain, but I must take exception and the very strongest exception, to any provision authorizing the ordering of cars to places where grain is damp and thereby liable to become damaged in accordance with the amendment made to the Manitoba Grain Act and to this further provision that cars may be ordered:
Whenever, after due examination, the board considers it necessary and advisable in order to relieve congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain.
In the first case-that of sending cars specially to places where there is damaged grain-I consider that the provisions now in the section to deal with elevators in danger of collapse and elevators in which grain is in danger of heating go as far as it is safe for the Act to go. When we have provided, as we have provided in the case of the Manitoba Grain Act, that cars may be specially ordered to any locality where grain is damp, and liable thereby to become damaged, we have not dealt wisely with the condition as it actually prevails in this very season, because the condition prevails in so many localities and these localities are so widely separated that if special orders be given in the interest of each locality where grain is damaged it practically means that there is no special advantage to any locality and the matter is reduced down to the point of that locality which is the greatest favourite, or puts up the best story, getting the advantage, which is an entirely undesirable condition of affairs.
I will admit that under this provision it would be possible to give relief in a certain locality, but in such a year as this, where the damage is extended over a wide area, the provision is aDsolutely valueless, and inasmuch as it introduces the possibility of favouritism, I object most strongly to this provision being incorporated in the Bill. I agreed to its being adopted as a part of the Manitoba Grain Act for this season without having given the subject the fullest consideration; it was represented to be a matter of urgency and we allowed the Bill to go through; but on fuller consideration I am prepared to take the fullest responsibility for the stand I take that this provision should not be embodied in this Bill which is supposed to be a permanent statute. The provision now proposed throws this whole question, which is the most critical connected with the whole administration

346S
of the Grain Act, absolutely on the discretion of the board. If we do this, without wishing to cast any reflection on the board, we have spent our time for nothing in providing the long and intricate list of regulations which comprise this Act. If you can afford to let the matter of car distribution go to the discretion of the board we may safely leave everything else to the same discretion. I would be bound to give the strongest opposition I could to the amendment now proposed, except that I would be willing to agree to an amendment that would allow of special orders of cars in the case of distribution of seed grain.

I know that I may be .criticised for what I am about to say, by the advisers whom we have coming from the west so frequently. The same organization who are taking such strong exception to any change in the present Grain Act as regards distribution of cars, have always been very anxious that in constituting such a board as this, we should have an independent board. Where are they going to get their independence, if you surround them with legislation that prohibits them from moving one inch to the right or to the left except by special Act of parliament. Certain districts in the west are suffering because they cannot get their crops to market, and if an independent board has the right to go to that particular locality, and as this Act provides to investigate, to make a thorough investigation, then such a locality could get relief. And why should the board not be permitted to give them relief without coming here and asking parliament, which would take probably a whole session; the board should have that much independence, and if they are not anxious to relieve the people's sufferings to the greatest extent then they are not fit and proper persons to be on that board.
My hon. friend has no objection to the seed grain portion of the Bill but he objects with regard to the damp grain. The law before Bill (No. 96) provided belief for whom? For the elevator man whose elevator was collapsing, whose grain was rotting or spoiling, or heating. Was there any relief for the farmer who might have on his farm 5,000 to 10.000 bushels of grain heating or spoiling? Bill (No. 96) provides that such a man can get relief, the same relief as the elevator man. That portion of Bill (No. 96) which deals with damp wheat or wheat that is geing wrong, should be incorporated in this Grain Act. I cannot see any objection to incorporating the whole of it. i shall certainly support the minister in the amendments he has proposed.

So far the committee have been verv harmonious. We have had Mr. OLIVER.
division on only one matter, the name of the wheat, which was more a question of opinion than of principle, and I want to congratulate hon. gentlemen opposite that so far -they have shown a desire to meet the wishes of the grain growers for whom this Bill is in the first instance framed. On this question, however, we seem to part. The question between the western members on the government side and those on this side is whether we are going to give effect to the opinion and desire expressed to us by the organized representatives of the grain growers who constitute the great majority of our electors and without question constitute the foundation of the whole country in the west at least, There is no question as to what the grain growers in the west want. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I aim sure, have received representations from many constituents requesting that they should support the view expressed by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I would not be outside the mark if I said that they had received no representations to the contrary. As far as we are in a position to know the wishes of our constituents at this distanci we believe their desires to be that there should be no radical changes in these clauses in connection with the distribution of cars.
My hon. friend from Macdonald says he wants to give this board powers so" that they will be able to turn a little to the right and to the left. I have no objection to giving them power to turn to the right, but I do not want to give them power to make a blunder some day and turn to the left. There might be some occasion when they would do good by exercising this discretion. There is no Cabinet ininis-tei or ex-C*binet minister in Canada vbo will question this statement, that in the administration of the laws of parliament or the regulations of a department, there are cases	in which	it would	be in	thepublic	interest	to depart	from	thelaw or regulation. In the administration	of the lands in the	west I haveknown	many a	case in	which	the
homestead regulations bore heavily on a man, but at the same time the parliament of Canada is governing, not one man simply, but seven or eight millions of people, and we must adopt legislation which in the long run and -on the large scale is going to be for the advantage of the great masses of the people. Would it be to the advantage of the grain trade of the west and of the people of Canada generally to have this clause inserted in this Act? I submit that it would not. I submit that it would be a step in a backward direction. This protection was only put on our statute-book after years of agitation by our farmers for this car distribution. It is not wholly satisfactory but it

is in the right direction, and it would be a reactionary step to take away that protection.

The old Act made provision for the elevator man whose grain was spoiling. I suppose the hon. gentleman is in favour of that part of the old Act, as it stood. Is he opposed to giving the farmer whose grain may be spoiling on the farm the same relief?

I am entirely in favour of giving the farmer the relief which my hon. friend thinks he refers to, but which he is mistaken about, Before I sit down I wish to read a few resolutions of the farmers, who are intelligent, and who know as well as my hon. friend does what relief they need. I will first read an official _ extract from the Grain Growers' Association of the province of Alberta, signed by the secretary, Edward J. Fream. He says:
It has been rumoured that section 207 of the Grain Bill will be considerably changed. This section is, we consider, one of the most important in the Act and one on which considerable time and attention should be bestowed before allowing any changes to be made. It gives a privilege to the farmer which is his only safeguard against the elevator interests, and while a determined onslaught has repeatedly been made upon this provision, yet the opponents of same have never yet been able to present any logical argument why a change should be made. Before this clause was added to the Grain Act the farmers were completely at the mercy of the interests, and if the clause is removed or in any way weakened bv dangerous amendments which might be made to give two different meanings, conditions will be such that iu a short time the farmers would find the car distribution and the general treatment they would receive from the railway companies and the elevator interests even more intolerable than they were before the clause was introduced into the Act.
I attach a great deal of importance to such an expression as this, as I am sure the minister will. It is my duty also to inform the House of the representations from the associations of farmers in my own constituency. Here is one from the Milden Grain Growers' Association, in the northern part of the Mooseiaw district. I will not read the whole of the preamble':
Whereas many statements made in the said petition are untrue and misleading; and
Whereas any change made in the car distribution clauses of the Manitoba Grain Act, would be unfair and detrimental to both the large and small farming interests of this province; therefore
Resolved, that the Milden Grain Growers Association condemns the petition of the Canadian Credit Men's Association, and earnestly requests that no change be made in the aforesaid clauses of the Manitoba Grain Act; and
Further resolved, that the secretary of this association be instructed to send copies of this resolution to the Hon. R. L. Borden, Premier of Canada, Hon. Geo. E. Foster, Minister of Trade and Commerce, and to Mr. Knowles, representative of this constituency.
C. MILLS, President.
E. W. HENRY, Secretary.
The following is from Boldenhurst, in the northern part of my riding and further west:
At a meeting of the Boldenhurst Branch of the Grain Growers' Association, the following motion was unanimously carried:-
It was moved by Wilbert Haggarty and seconded by James Parsons, that this association strongly disapproves of any change being made in tlio Manitoba Grain Act in regard to the distribution of cars.

I have received a communication from a constituent -of mine who is a very representative man, Mr. A. Bryan, of Bridge-ford, as follows:
Dear Sir,-I have addressed to the Hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce a strong protest against the petition that I understand has been presented to him by the Credit Men's Association of Winnipeg. The object of this is not to help the small farmers, as it is claimed to be, but to further the interests of tlie elevator people. The small farmer who lias not a carload of grain to ship lias not asked for it and does not want it. Most of these men here got some at least of their grain into the elevators, while quite a few small farmers who have just a carload to ship have not as yet been able to get a car.
The result of suspending clause 99 of the Manitoba Grain Act would be to compel these men to sell to the elevators. Now it is notorious in the west that the elevators rob the farmers all ends and sides. Not only is there a difference in price of between 5 and 10 cents per bushel between Port Arthur and street prices, but the wheat is knocked down a grade; it is docked extortionately and oftentimes proper weight is not given. On behalf of 200 farmers of the Bridgeford district I emphatically protest against it. Great consternation has been caused in regard to the said petition, and should it be regarded favourable bv the government, it might cause considerable friction, even rioting, as the farmers are determined not to have their rights infringed upon.
And they trust, you, as their representative, will make a strong protest when the matter is brought up.
I will now read a telegram from a western farmer, than whom there is none better in Canada. I refer to Mr. Fred W. Green, secretary of the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association. The message is as follows:
Moosejaw Sask., Feb., 9, 1912. IV. E. Knowles, M.P., Ottawa.
Received many letters this morning signed Credit Association. Petition under misapprehension. Asked to have names removed. Holders of petition refuse. Asking me what they can do. Farmers generally denouncing Credits. Mean underhand trick.
(Sgd.) FRED W. GREEN, .
Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association.
Speaking for myself I have never had any other representation but one side of the question. I have had no constituent ask me to change to the other side. If the constituents of other hon. gentlemen have requested them to take the stand Mr. KNOWLES.
they took well and good, it is their business; but for myself there is no possible doubt in my mind as to the stand I must take viz: That this matter be not changed in the radical way in which the minister desires it should be changed.
I am rather ignorant about the matter. Would the hon. gentleman give me a specific case where the farmers will be damaged by the enforcement of the proposed amendment?

In regard to this matter it is feared that a peril would be constantly hanging over the grain growers by reason of the power held by the three men who constitute that board. It is feared that from influences that were not in the interest of the country, tne board might order a distribution of cars that would prejudice some and unduly favour others.
I would like to get an instance of that if I could.
I could not do that because the board is not yet born, and I do not believe in original sin to that extent.
The farmers must have instances in view, I should think of what might happen.
Yes.
Then I would like to have instances of that.

I think I might answer that question in a brief way by saying that you place great power in the hands of three men. They will doubtless be respectable men, and men of ability, but I have not the least doubt also that they will be strong party men. It is possible they would be subject to influences that are not the highest and noblest-my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has been long enough in politics to know what I mean-and they might order a distribution of cars which would not be in the interest of .the grain glowers. Therefore, there is a feeling of danger which overshadows the hopes of our grain growers if that power is allowed to rest in the hands of the board. The member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) says whv not give them the power to turn to the' right or to the left. I stood up in this liouse" when we were framing the section of the Bill providing that the board be given power to make regulations, and I said I coul'd conceive that during the grain rush it might be necessary to make regulations without obtaining the consent of the minister or the consent of the Governor in Council. But me government would not give them even that little power. They said:	' Nothing. Every change in
the regulations which this Board of Grain Commissioners make must be approved, not only by the minister but by the Gov-

lernor in Council. They take the stand that they want the board to possess such wide powers and yet they are tying thejr hands. So strictly I say that with regard to this very essential and vital matter in the operation of this Act there should be no taking away from the farmer the protection that he is enjoying the benefit of.

I would ask the hon. gentleman before he sits down whether he is in favour, or his friends on that side, of the House of incorporating Bill (No. 96) as we passed it in reference to damp grain in this Act?
I would have to read the Act over agin.

This is the Bill that we inserted and it is now law:
Subsection 1 of section 99b of the Manitoba Grain Act, chapter 83 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, as the said subsection is enacted by section 4.1 of chapter 45 of the Statutes of 1908, is amended by inserting after the word ' collapse in the third line thereof, the words ' to places where grain is damp and liable to become damaged, or for the purpose of distributing seed grain to any point in the western division.'
Are hon. gentleman opposite in favour of incorporating that Bill in the Act?
If the hon. gentleman wants to make it permanent for all the year, and every season of the year, I say no, I am not in favour of it.

The hon. gentleman understands my meaning. I believe that the Act is a fair and legitimate one and I am in favour of it. I have received a number of letters and petitions from the farmers throughout my district asking me to exert to the utmost any influence I could, to prevent any change in the clause which refers to the distribution of cars. I received no petitions or letters to the contrary. 1 think there is something in the suggestion of my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples), that the fears entertained as to what would occur under the operation of the clause are more imaginery than real. The member for South York (Mr. Maclean) asked for an instance of where this ivould do damage. As the law is not operative yet it is not possible to give an exact instance; but the reason, I understand, why the farmers in my district object to any change is that in 1902, 1906 and in 1908 there were certain amendments made to the clause referring to the distribution of cars, and all the time they have been asking to be put in a position which they believe to be in their interest. The farmers believed they were subject to the influence of certain interests-it may be railway interests, elevator interests or other interests -and, rightly or wrongly, they feel that 110
the clause as we have it in the Manitoba Grain Act is in their interest. Now, in my opinion, if there was not some suspicion, justly entertained perhaps, that the interests were again operating in the belief that the matter had gone too far in favour of the farmers and against the railways and the elevators, they would not be sending us these petitions. This Bill, with the exception of clause (e), I am prepared to accept, and to defend before the farmers of my district. I believe it is in the interest not only of the farmers but of the country, that we should have Bill (No. 96) incorporated in this Act, and the other provisions of the amendment that the Minister of Trade and Commerce sees fit to introduce. But I must say-I cannot help saying-that I am a little afraid of clause (e). If it does not go any further than it says, well and good-and after all perhaps that is the only argument one has a right to make, that it means what it says-but I know that the arguments of the farmers will be that it is the thin edge of the wedge.
This subsection (e) reads:
When after due examination the board considers it necessary and desirable, in order to relieve congestion and facilitate the despatch of grain.
Now, if it always remained there, I believe the farmers would not so seriously object to this subsection. And I would not have it thought that I lack faith in the commission that is to be appointed or in the efficiency of this Bill as a working measure. We have been in committee on this Bill for some days, and, as my hon. friend was good enough to say-and we can all agree with him-this has been a very amicable committee and we have ground out what, I believe will be a splen-dit Grain Bill in the interest of this country. But this is the one clause which the farmers in my 'constituency do not feel fully satisfied about. Perhaps, for the reasons I stated a while ago they may have good reasons to be fearful of something that might occur if such broad powers as are proposed under this subsection were given to this commission. To repeat what I said before so far as the other clauses- are concerned, I am in full sympathy with them. My hon. friend from Edmonton, (Mr. Oliver) does not seem to be billing to go so far. But I am prepared to go upon the platform in my constituency, and support these clauses, as being in the best interests of the farmers, all except this one. I think it was the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), who said that a farmer might have 5,000 bushels of grain in his granary spoiling, because of damp or of some other reason. Surely it would be of advantage to that farmer if the commission , had the powers, although he had had his

car, to grant him the privilege of receiving another car. Still, so far as this subsection (e) is concerned, I do not feel that I am in a position to favour so broad an extension of the powers of the commission as this would seem to give. I am strongly in favour of the other clauses, but this subsection (e) I could hardly support without further light.
Keep an open mind.
Yes, I will keep an open mind.

I should like to endorse what has fallen from my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) as well as my hon. friends from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) as to the universality of opinion on this subject among the farmers so far as we can gather from the communications sent to us. Personally, I have for years laid well to heart the teaching of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr-Foster) as to the importance of mixed farming. I am not immediately concerned with grain farming, preferring to deliver my grain on foot. 1 have no very strong opinion on this question nor any intimate knowledge of it. But I have an intimate (knowledge of the university (of Opinion which prevails amongst those who do know about it. This is not a party question at all. I had a letter a few days ago from a man who, so far as I know, never gave anything but a Conservative vote in his life until the last election, when he had the good sense, according to my view, to vote for reciprocity, and he spoke about this provision as^ being the last straw that would break the camel s back. Similar expressions occur in other communications that I have received. That would appear to indicate that the anen who are concerned, the men irrespective of party who are growing this grain, have been well served by the state of things as it is. I have not the remotest doubt that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) has brought to bear on this question what he brings to bear upon everything, a passionate desire to know the full details and to do what he believes to be best under the circumstances. I am sorry, on that account, that I have to differ from him on this question. But the representations are so unanimous from those who are concerned that I have no option. I agree with my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver).

The question before the committee is worthy of the most serious attention of which we are capable. I have no fault to find with the statements
Mr. SHEPHERD
of fact as generally presented by hon. gentlemen opposite, namely, that there is a very unanimous sentiment in the west against any radical change in section 108 of the Act, and the general provisions referring to car distribution. At the same time, the reasons which I have received, and indeed the reasons so far as they have been presented to the House by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) do not appear to conflict with the principle or with the details of the amendment proposed by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). The position taken by the organized farmers is that the ground gained some years ago and largely, I believe, as a result of their own agitation-shall not now be lightly surrendered or lost. To' my mind, this Bill does not go one step towards the surrendering any of that ground. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) seemed to try to get at the root of the principle involved, and I think, he saw it; but I think he shunned the logical result because he feared it might lose to him some political advantage that he seemed to think in sight.
Now, what is this clause? In former years in this country the rights of property were magnified, they were considered so sacred that public rights frequently were disregarded. And in no case did this idea of private rights predominate more than in the case of the railway companies. One of these rights was considered to be that of placing their rolling stock where they wished, and of carrying the grain as seemed to them most convenient. But parliament came to see in time that the public had a vested interest in this matter _ as well as the railway company, and parliament took upon itself to say by what rule the cars should be distributed. They declared that John Jones who orders first, and William Smith who orders next, and elevator ' B that orders next shall receive cars in this order. That was ground gained so far as it went, and so far as it has gone it has worked out to the advantage of the western farmer. The railway has not been able to dictate, since that was enforced, what they should do with what they considered their own property rights. The amendments proposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) instead of being a (surrender, in my opinion is an advance on this principle. It declares that the general rule laid down shall still be followed, that parliament having once assumed the right to say how this should be done in a general way, still stands to that right; but parliament declares not only for that right in itself, but also that the commission appointed under the authority of parliament, the representatives of the public interest and the public need, shall be able to

enforce that right. Hon. members opposite conceded the whole principle when they conceded Bill (No 96), they conceded the force of the argument presented and the conditions that demand a change which have been brought forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. '
But now they recoil, and all they can advance to surround themselves is that they received certain resolutions. Why? Because the farmers have been taught to believe, Whether rightly or wrongly,- that there is going to be a surrender, there is going to be a step backward, and that all tne ground gained back in 1907 is. to be miyerL T1^*. That is not the case at all. The principle of the resolution read by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) shows that if they understood what is nro-P.osed to be done, there would be no opposition. What does Mr. Fream say? In the body of the memorial presented by him, this appears:
While it may be possible to provide for permission being given to the commission after investigation to supply cars for seed grain, or upon petition of farmers for the removal of wet or damaged grain, or where there was suffering through a shortage of fuel or food supplies, yet if there is any chance of the rights of the farmers being infringed by ambiguous or vaguely worded amendments introduced into the Bill, it will he better for our interests as producers for the clause to Temain as it now stands.
. Now Mr. Fream states the whole thing; in other words, he says that the better way is to leave the law as it stands and to follow the general rule just as it was, but, if, to the advantage of the farmer, it can be shown that it should bend in individual cases, that is all the bettter, provided the clause is clearly and not vaguely worded. That indicates the stand taken by the western farmer.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that clause (e) goes further?

It goes no further in principle at all. But the commissioners would require to he convinced that the farmers' interest was served by a divergence. You can never, by an individual statement of contingencies, state them all. There may be something which we do not conceive in this committee, and to make it advisable that the gtrict provisions of 198 should be made to bend in the interest of a certain community, clause (e) is neither more nor less than saying that if we have not succeeded in stating what classes and contingencies may occur, then the clause shall give the commission power to go beyond. Now the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says that if you give the commission this power, you might just as well burn the Grain Act, and he says we llOi
are appointing a commission who shall superintend the grain trade of this country. Now what is the logical position of the member for Edmonton? What is the principle of the Grain Act? It provides a machinery that shall take care of the distribution and the outlet of the western giain, the grading of it, and so forth; it provides machinery for handling the grain tiade of this country. Then it appoints a commission to superintend that machinery, and it says to them:	There is the
