Further consideration in Committee of the Whole of Bill (No. 84) respecting certain patents of Thomas D. Rambaut.-Mr. Ames.
On section 2-power to receive petitions and make orders.

Mr. Chairman, before this section is adopted I want to direct the attention of the committee to something that perhaps is not very apparent on the face of the Bill as it stands. The committee Mr. MEIGHEN.
will remember that when this was up, I think a week ago to-night, I asked the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, (Mr. Ames) who has charge of this Bill, if he knew whether these patents, as originally issued, came under the provisions of section 44 of the Patent Act. The hon. gentleman stated that he was not in a position to give me that information. I wrote to Mr. Lynch, chief of the patent office, and, a few days ago, received this communication:
Ottawa, Feb. 16, 1912.
My dear Mr. Carvell,
In reply to your question over the telephone this afternoon, relative to a number of patents granted to E. W. Cooke and assigned to one Rambaut, I beg to say that none of the patents have been under section 44 of the Patent Act (compulsory license system).
Tours very sincerely,
(Sgd.) W. J. LYNCH
Chief of Patent Office.
F. B. Carvell, Esq., M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Just consider for a moment what the promoters of this Bill are asking parliament to do for them. By section 38 of the Patent Act, which has been the law of the land for many years, it is provided that in order to hold a patent, the patentee, either directly or through some other person, must actually commence the manufacture of the patented article in Canada within two years of the granting of the patent. He must do more than that; he must have the article ready to be sold to any person who applies for it at a reasonable price and continually be in that position, or, to read the section, it is as follows :
Such patent, and all the rights and privileges thereby granted shall cease and determine, and the patent shall he null and void at the end of two years from the date thereof, unless the patentee or his legal representatives, within that period or an authorized extension thereof, commence, and after such commencement, continuously carry on in Canada the construction or manufacture of the invention patented, in such a manner that any person desiring to use it may obtain it or cause it to be made for inm at a reasonable price at some manufactory or establishment for making or constructing it in Canada.
That was found, in some instances, to work a hardship. I could give an illustration wherein it would work a hardship. A man might invent a complicated piece of machinery-we will say a certain kind of steam engine, or machinery for the making of some particular, specified article. Take, for instance, a printing press, or anything that you could imagine of which there are not many sales in Canada. It might cost a large amount of money to equip the factory and put it in a position to manufac-

ture this and possibly, when you equipped the factory and had manufactured one or two articles, it might be a number of years before you found sale for more than those two articles. The result would be an enormous loss. In that case many people have failed to keep their patents alive by manufacturing them simply because the initial expenditures in getting ready to manufacture and being in a position to keep on manufacturing the patented article have been so great that they did not feel that they could afford to undertake it. Therefore, in 1903, parliament attempted to get around that difficulty by passing section 44 of the Patent Act as it now stands, and which was codified in the revision of 1906. It is the law of the land to-day. Section 44 provides, speaking generally, that if, in the judgment of the commissioner of patents, an article patented comes within the class I have described, something which it would not be fair or reasonable to expect the patentee to be manufacturing all the time and to be in a position to sell to any Iverson who wants it, then the commissioner of patents has the right to give him a license so that he will not be compelled to manufacture, but he must hold himself in readiness to lease to any other person who wants to manufacture the article at any time, and if they cannot agree upon the royalty to be paid for the right then the commissioner of patents is appointed arbitrator in the matter.
But when this man Rambaut, or his predecessor in title, applied fox his patents and his patents were issued, they were not brought within the conditions of section 44 of the Act of 1903, and section 44 was the law of the land, then as it is to-day. Anyone can readily understand why these patents were not brought under the provisions of section. 44. They did not apply to a complicated piece of machinery, 'they were not regarding an article which might never be sold to customers because it was not like a 'Complicated steam' engine. They had reference to a method of making a certain kind of food-you might call it dtes-sicated food-something that would be sold, if sold at all, to thousands and tens' of thousands of people. If the invention had any use whatever it would be that an. industry would be established or the patent would be sold to other people who would be producing all over the country the article covered by it. The faon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, when this measure was before the committee on a former occasion, took the ground that if we refused this patent we would possibly be .preventing the establishment of an industry in Canada. I want to point out to the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, and the members of this committee that if we pass this Bill as it is drawn, and if we ratify
*section 2, we are defeating the very object that the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, claimed to have in view when he asked us in 'the 'committee last week to pass this Bill for him. lie said: Refuse to pass this Bill and you will probably prevent the establishment of an industry in Canada. I say that if you pass this Bill as it stands to-night, without any question whatever, you will, prevent the establishment of an industry in Canada. You will be giving the owner of this patent the right to hold his patent for the remainder of the term of 18 years, which I think would be about 13 years longer, and hie may never expend a dollar in Canada either directly or indirectly. He will never have to expend a dollar upon any manufacturing establishment, he will never have to employ a man, until the expiration, of 13 years, and still his patent will Ibe perfectly good. All he has to do is to hold himself in readiness to say: I will give any man the right to manufacture this article providing he pays me 'my royalty. I am. satisfied that the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, cannot gainsay one 'Statement I have made, because T have given you the law on the matter and I do submit that this Bill should not be passed. If we have to renew this man's patents, surely this committee ought only to renew them like an ordiuOTy patent under section 1. We should not give this man something which he did not have when he got his original patent. They are asking the parliament of Canada not only to give him something which he bad lost by this negligence, but they are asking parliament to give him something which he never thought of holding when be got the patent. The most that can be said is that he had a perfect right, if the commissioner of patents had thought proper, to have had the patent brought under the provisions of section 44, but, because it did not come under the provisions of section 44 I think it is only fair to assume that the commissioner of patents did not consider that it was a case that should have come under the provisions of that section. I have no knowledge of that myself and all I can say is that it looks that way to me. Now, they are asking parliament to put this man in a position that the commissioner of patents would not put him in. Therefore, I do submit that section 2 should be defeated because it is bad enough to give- an American who has no interest in Canada the right to continue this monopoly and this sort of business, but it is going too far when parliament is asked to continue a monopoly under which the beneficiary will never be compelled to spend a dollar or employ a man. in Canada.

My hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) a week ago and also to-night has endeavoured to create

the feeling that this Bill should not pass because the patentee is an American.
I never made such a statement at any time.
That was the inference.
I did not say so.

I leave it to the judgment of the House if the whole tenor of the hon. gentleman's remarks was not to the effect that he would like to stir up prejudice against the applicant in this case because he was an American and a stranger. Our Canadian patent laws make absolutely no discrimination against members of any nationality, a German, an Englishman, an American, has the same rights to patent as a Canadian. That argument of my hon. friends the House will dispose of. once and for all as unworthy of its consideration.
I differ from my hon. friend's interpretation of a portion of the Patent Act. Under the original patent the patentee had the right to proceed under section 38 or section 44. Section 38 makes the patent conditional upon his manufacturing in Canada within two years.
I spoke to Mr. Lynch and I have his letter stating that this applicant did not come under section 44. If Mr. Lynch has misinformed me, I have misinformed the House.

I shall make the matter clear. Section 38 provides that the patent is conditional upon manufacturing within two years and not importing after that time. Section 44 declares the conditions which may be substituted for section 38 in the judgment of the officers. Under that section the patentee may give a license to others to manufacture. Clause 2 of the present Bill does not ask parliament to give this man the rights he originally had in their entirety. This clause simply says that he has the right of patent and the Commissioner of Patents, an official of the government, shall determine whether he can make out a sufficient case to have it declared that he shall have the privileges of section 44. If the Commissioner of Patents is of opinion that it is not advisable to give him the rights under section 44 the commissioner will say so. Inasmuch as the patentee, in the first place, had rights under both section 38 and 44, and purely through a misunderstanding he lost his rights and as this House has affirmed in the second reading that the principle is sound, it only remains for us to settle the terms on which the restoration of rights shall be made. My contention is that he should be given full rights, namely Mr. AMES.
to act either conditionally under section 38, or section 44, at the discretion of the commissioner. He now asks for two years more within which to commence manufacture. If the House says that he shall not have this privilege then I hope that the House will hold to that precedent and deal in the same way -with everyone else who comes here and asks for the restoration of a patent. This Bill asks that he be put back in the place he was in originally, the place he lost through no fault of his own.
The House has repeatedly granted relief to applicants who have forfeited certain rights. In 1909 the House passed five Bills of this character, introduced in every case by supporters of the government and in only one instance did the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) object. Last session, a number of others were passed, several of the applicants being Americans. While hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side of the House they agreed to Bills of this character, four or five of them every session. All these patents were restored although the fees had not been paid and they were restored for six years. In this case all fees had been paid for six years and it will be still another year before the time elapses so far as fees are concerned. These parties did not manufacture, that is all they failed to do.
They ask the opportunity within the next two years of establishing a manufactory here. If that opportunity is given them they will establish it, I thoroughly believe. If they are deprived of the opportunity, that industry will not come to Canada. It is not to be expected that an industry of this character will come to Canada if it is not protected in its patent Tights. I do not think people will invest money in an industry requiring any expenditure of capital if they can have no security that the man next door will not immediately imitate their process. They must be protected for a certain length of time. Now, this patent has lapsed, and parliament is asked to restore it. I do not know why exception should be taken to that request in this particular case. We have already passed three Bills of the same character, two of which have passed the Senate; but for some reason this particular Bill has been selected, and every possible objection is made to it.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the Bill that passed here the other night is at all of the same character as this Bill?

Yes, very much indeed. On two of the Bills the fees nave not been paid, so nothing had been done. In this case the fees have been paid for six

years, from 1907 to 1913. The one requirement of manufacture was not complied with, but the parties interested will be very glad to comply with it if they are given another opportunity. I have not gone into the special reasons why Mr. Rambaut did not originally comply with all the provisions of the Patent Act. These were all given to the House a week ago. Inasmuch as the second reading, which involves the principle, has passed, and inasmuch as the Bill has unanimously passed the Private Bills Committee, and inasmuch as the preamble and the first clause, the essential parts of the Bill, have passed, I can only say that if the House desires to restore the Rambaut patent to the position it originally occupied, it will pass clause 2. But if the House decides that a man who allows his patent to lapse, and who comes here to have it reinstated, shall not have the privileges he first had, it will strike out clause 2, and he will have to be content with clause 1.
In this case he asked for three months.
But you have not done it for five years.
Does my hon. friend allege that on the 7th of May, 1907, when this man took out these letters patent, he had not the two options?
He had until the 7th of September, 1907, and that date went by.
What this Bill asks is that he be put back where he was on the 7th of May, 1907.
Why should he be?
Why should he not be?

He allowed the 7th of September, 1907, to go by, and put it on the 27th of September, 1907, and there is no power on earth that can give him the right to come under section 44. Therefore, the argument of my hon. friend is fallacious.

I understand that he took out his patent on the 7th of May, 1907. If within six months thereafter he had applied to come under clause 44, he might have done so.
Therefore for six months at least we had the advantage we speak of here. Clause 2 of this Bill says:	that notwithstanding
anything in the Patent Act, or in the patents mentioned in the preamble, the commissioner of patonibsi may within three months give the patentee the right to exercise the title which he had for six months following 7th of May, 1907. If he does not exercise it within six months he never can exercise it at all; he cannot exercise it during the whole year as the hon. member alleges*. We are, therefore, only giving him, as far as time is concerned, the right to: exercise the title which he had under sections 38 and 44 of the Patent Act.
He would not have the light to come under section 44 within the six months unless he had the right to apply, and the commissioner would have power to say whether he should come in.
It is the same in both cases. That is exactly the case here.
But that right has gone four years ago.
It is exactly the same in both cases. He has the right to apply and if the commissioner will not accept his application that is the end of it.

My hon. friend is entirely out of court so far as section 44 is

concerned. If this man had gone back to the patent office he could not have got the right. How does he propose to get it? He sleeps until he is out of court entirely and his patent is no good. Then he comes back to parliament and says: ' I have been remiss in my duty and have not done that which the law required me to do and I want you not only to put me back in the position'I was in two years ago, but to put me in the position I would have been in if I had applied four years ago. My hon. friend is not serious in trying to make this committee believe the man is not asking something which he has no right to ask. My hon. friend says we will be preventing the establishment of a manufactory in Canada, and that if we do not put this Bill through,
' nobody will have the right to manufacture here the article covered by the patent.

Would my hon. friend
meet the argument from this point: Is not this man Rambaut's right to be restored to his original position just on the same footing as that he has a right to he restored to the patent? That is to say he claims the right to get back his patent on the ground of an error. If that is good is he not also entitled to get back his option?

No, the only thing he would have a right to do would be to ask us to replace him in the position which he occupied the day his patent was voided or ceased to be of any value. Now, his patent ceased to be of any value on the 7th day of May, 1907, or on the 7th day of May, 1909. Therefore, on the 7th day of May, or we will say on the 6th day of May, 1909, he did not posses the right of applying to the commissioner on patents under section 44 for the right to manufacture. I do not think we ought to put him in a better position than he was in on the 7th of May, 1907. But if section 2 of this Bill be passed we are placing him in the position he occupied four years ago, we are placing a premium on the man's own negligence. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) stated that if you do not recognize this as the man's patent you may forever prevent the establishment of the industry in Canada. Does he not understand that if the patent has expired every man in Canada has a right to start this industry? It is a monopoly my hon. friend is trying to create, and if this Bill be not passed that monopoly is abolished. My hon. friend is interested in mergers, therefore his mind is running in the direction of monopolies. My hon. friend says that within the last few _ years many patents have been revived, but can he point to an instance where a patent has been revived giving back to the man something he did not possess at the time the patent was void? The Wadge case Mr. CARVELL
has been referred to as an illustration. In that case the patent became void because Wadge had not paid the $15. A patent is given to a man in order to protect the genius of his brain and he has two years in which to commence the manufacture of that article in Canada. If he chooses to do so he can pay $60 and he gets an 18 year certificate If he only pays $20 he gets six years protection. In the case of Wadge it was a matter of paying only $15 or $20 because he was manufacturing the article, had been doing so for many years, and had a big business in Winnipeg. This man Rambaut has never spent a dollar in Canada on the manufacture of the article for which he desires to revive the patent.

I am sorry the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) thought it necessary to introduce party feeling into a question of this kind. His evident purpose was to arouse his partisans to support his case, whether the law or the practice would sustain him or not.
Order.

Yes, I am in order. It would be a pity if private rights of this character should be subject in this House to party sentiment or party bigotry; and I think that for a member of the age and experience in this House of the hon. member for St. Antoine to introduce such an idea into the discussion of such a Bill as itihis is liatheir ia pity. The hon. mieimiher for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) wanted us to disregard entirely the limitation of the statutes. There are limitations in this statute. There is what is well known in this country as the statute of limitations, dealing with the question of debts. An hon. member on the other side, let us say, loaned his neighbour $1,000 in cash, taking the man's note for it, and put the note in his safe. Through some misunderstanding, he has allowed more than six years to go by before trying to collect the debt. And when he asks for the money, the debtor, dishonest man as he is, says: You cannot collect the money because it is more than six years since I got it, and I will not give it to you.
Is there any tiling in that to prevent the statute of limitations from running?

There 'are so many that it would take too long-ias time is short- to tell them to my ihon. friend.
Mr. MIDDiLBBRO. Does not the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) think that the debtor ought to be paid the $1,000 notwithstanding the lapse of time?

Certainly. But the statute of limitations! is there, and the creditor cannot collect. There is a statute of limitations here and one is no more insuperable than the other. Suppose that the creditor in this case were to come to this House and say: This dishonest man is depriving me of $1,000; he has built a house with it and is living in the house; and I want you to remove the statute of limitations in this case so that I may collect my $1,000, he would have no chance of succeeding; in fact, I do not think there is an hon. member of this House who would introduce the Bill. Everybody would say:
Such a request is an absurdity; this is the law of the land, and you have to take your medicine. That being our attitude in one case, why should the hon. gentleman propose that we should iset aside so lightly the limitations in this case ? Whatever the genius of this man's brain has made is now the property of the country. The hon, gentleman must know that. His rights under the statutes have lapsed, the limitation clause of the statute having done its work.
What wias the attitude of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) toward the previous Bill? ?
That was all explained on the reading of the preamble a week ago, if the hon. member had been here.

I was here. But the hon. gentleman did not say in his explanation where the mistake of law was. He told us there was a dispute between the heirs of one Cooke, and the person now holding this right. He did not explain how it was*, or how it was contended that Cooke had not got a proper title. If the hon. member comes to me as one member of the committee and tells me that he wants to perfect a title which he has received, I will vote with him, but I do not

feel that I am called on to support a man who slept on his rights, because he got some mistaken idea of the law and now comes to parliament to put him back, and give him what is to-day the property of the country to which he has no right. I have not heard any satisfactory explanation of what the difficulty was that prevented him from completing his title.

It seems to me that if the hon. member (Mr. Ames), would amend this legislation to put the man who had the patent in exactly the same position as he was in when he lost his. patent rights through not carrying out the terms on which those rights were granted -manufacturing the article in question, in Canada within a given time-if he would amend it so as to give this man exactly what he lost when his patent became void, then I do not think there would be anyi objection on the part of anybody in this House to reinstate his patent.

I have been asking that he be given all that he had when he took out his patent. If hon. gentlemen think that is too much, will they pass the Bill if we strike out clause 2, and leave him in the position he was when his patent lapsed?

Certainly.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 32) respecting grain-Mr. Foster (North Toronto).
On section 207,-distribution of cars,

organization asking me to support any amendment that may be introduced. It may be said by my hon. friends that the farmers do not understand what this amendment means. I am not prepared to say that that may not ue the reason in some cases. At the same time, as I said at the outset, I believe that the people of western Canada who have been shipping grain for twenty-five or thirty years and who have gone through the whole history of the development of the Grain Act and the question of car distribution, are in a far better position to express their opinion on these matters than any member of the Canadian Credit Men's Association located with headquarters in the city of Winnipeg can be. Let me refer to two or three representations that have been made to me. They do not differ to any extent from the representations that have been referred to by other members but they come from my own district and for that reason I wish to bring them to the attention of the committee. We the directors and members of the Craik Grain Growers' Association, and business men of the town of Craik, protest against any alteration in the Manitoba Grain Act, re distribution of cars as provided in section 99, clauses (a) (b) and (c) and that the present method of distribution of cars to the farmer has not been the cause of the blockade in wheat and the business of the country at a standstill as the petition circulated by the Canadian Credit Men's Association of Winnipeg has stated, and we further protest against the distribution of cars to be left to the Tailway commission.

Now I have given the opinion of the grain growers in opposition to the change in -the car distribution clause of the Manitoba Grain Act, and I would urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce to seriously consider the position of the western farmers not only individually but speaking collectively through -their association against any change in the Act. They prefer to have it remain as it is. They had this clause inserted in the Grain Act some years ago, and think that it should remain there without any change whatever. The opinion of the farmers in my constituency is against any change, and I am bound to -support that view because the farmers know more of what is necessary for their welfare than men who are not engaged in agriculture in western Canada.

I am not going to delay the House by reading a lot of resolutions, although I have received many petitions from my constituency, each and every one of them asking that no change^ whatever should be made in the -car distribution clause of the Act. This is the first controversial matter apparently that we have had in connection with this Bill, and the Minister of Trade -and Commerce has been most fair and reasonable all through. But the farmers -are now asking -to have matters left as they are. I do not think the Minister, after the interviews he has had with the members of the Grain Growers' Association of the west, would gainsay the fact that these men understand wheat growing and the handling of the western wheat crop as well as any other class of men in existence. The farmers of the -three prairie provinces are absolutely a unit in asking that no change should -be made in this clause. Who have we on the other side? We have the millers, the elevator men, the grain exchange men, the railroad men,

the Credit Men's Association-we have the corporate interests on one side asking for a change in the interests of the farmer. Why should they speak for the farmer? Cannot the farmer speak for himself?
Would the hon. gentleman tell us who these people have approached and asked for the change? I have never seen any of them.
Nor I.
Railroad men have been advocating that change to me half a dozen times. Grain exchange men here advocated a change upon a dozen occasions.
What change?
They have represented that the present system of car distribution is not right, and that it should be done away with or chahged.
They did not ask for this particular change, did they?

They did not ask for this particular change but they asked that the clause be changed, although the farmers are urging that it be left alone. This matter particularly affects the farmers and why do these interests come to individual members and ask that a change be made on the ground that it will help the small farmer who has not a fair deal under the present systeln of distribution of cars? I am not going to say that the present system of distribution may not work a hardship in the ease of individual farmers, but the present law is what the farmers as a whole have fought and worked for, for years. All they are asking now is that it be left alone. They are afraid that if any change is made, if any power is granted to anybody else to interfere with the present system of car distribution they will be the sufferers in the end. I absolutely concur in that view. Surely when the men who are chiefly interested in this matter are asking that the clause should stand as it is at present the least that can be done is to comply with their wishes? Suppose this power is given to a commission- and I am not going to make any reflections on any possible commission that may be appointed because I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce will appoint the best men he can find-what relief is going to be given in a season when there is a general blockade all over the country, by changing the system? If there should be demands coming in from 500 or 1,000 points, as there are at the present moment, it would be simply a matter of discriminating as to which point you should relieve. Why not leave this matter alone, and then if some of the farmers suffer in consequence it will simply be because their wishes were complied with and the responsibility will rest with them. The farmers through their association understand the subjects in my judgment just as well as any of these interests that are asking for the change. The grain growers associations throughout the west have proven within the last few years that they understand all questions in relation to the growing of wheat. So that I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce to withdraw clause (e). It has been claimed in this discussion that we have adopted this principle in supporting Bill (No. 96). I was in favour of that Bill and supported it with an accurate knowledge of what was doing, knowing that we gave the power in the meantime to deal with the present condition of affairs under which hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat are stacked up on the prairie, like coal, but knowing also that toe moment the Bill we are now dealing with became law, toe other measure would be repealed and be no longer of any effect. It is not fair for any one to advance toe argument that because we decided to pass that Bill in order to remedy an exceptional condition of affairs existing at this present moment, *that we were binding ourselves to relax the present system of car distribution for all time to come.
I had no such thought in my mind; and had I supposed that by passing that Bill, we should be held to be committing ourselves to the support of this amendement, I would not have voted for it. We have now a state of affairs in which the farmers ask for one thing and the interests which are generally supposed to be opposed to toe farmers, are asking for something else. as being opposed to aniy change in the oar distribution Clause of the Grain Act. Like a great many hon. members on both sides of the House, I have received personal letters from different electors in my constituency protesting against any change in these clauses. I have also been favoured [DOT]with resolutions from pretty nearly every Grain Growers' Association in my constituency adverse to this proposed 'change. Several of these Grain Growers' Associations have also written me stating that they have had Large petitions signed and forwarded to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), protesting against any change. As farmers we regard any change in this clause with a great amount of suspicion, I believe I am justified in making this statement. I have been growing wheat now for about eighteen years, and I can remember that about ten years ago the bankers, tihe railway companies anid the elevator people combined together anid refused to give the farmers oars 'to load their grain. The result was that the farmers were forced to ship their grain through the elevators or sell it to the elevators. This enabled the elevator men to lower the price of grain, and the result was that the spread between the street anid track price was about seven cents a bushel. You can readily see the loss that the farmers sustained as a result of that most unsatisfactory condition of affairs. The farmers succeeded in getting placed in the Act the present car distribution clauses and the result has been that within the past three or four years the spread between street and track has not exceeded two or three cents a bushel. Therefore, the farmers realize that they have derived great benefit from the car distribution clause as it is at present embodied in the Act. I, therefore, am strongly opposed to any change. It has been stated here that no person has asked for any change in this clause. If the privileged classes have not been asking for any change certainly the farmers have not asked for any, and, that being so, why make a change? This clause 207 gives the commission all the power that is- necessary. It gives the commission power to have cars provided if there is an elevator in danger of collapse or if there is any grain heating in the elevator. They can cause cars to be sent to different points to relieve such a situation as that. If power were given to the elevators to distribute seed grain I think that is all that is necessary and that is all the farmers are asking for. I want to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon the fair stand which he has taken all the way through in connection with this grain Bill and also members on both sides of the House. I may say that while I know a little about growv Mr. CRUISE.
ing wheat, I know very little about making laws with regard to shipping and selling wheat. I attended the committee meetings very regularly, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I derived a great deal of benefit from them. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in the interest of the producers of this country, to comply with their request and make no change in the Act. If the farmers came down to Toronto, that beautiful city that runs the whole country, and insisted on having anything to say to the manufacturers about the distribution of the cars upon which they load their machinery, the manufacturers would say to them:	What
business is it of yours? Go home to the west and mind your own affairs. I do not mean to say that it is none of their business, but the view I take of it is that this is purely and simply a farmer's question, and, therefore, the manufacturers of Toronto or anywhere else should not say how our grain should be loaded and shipped. Mr. Chairman, in common with every other hon. member from the west, I have received petitions and letters protesting against a change being made in this car distribution provision of the grain Act. The farmers in the district which I represent are not suffering in the same way that they are in other sections of western Canada, but at the same time they view with a great deal of alarm any change being made in the Act which has been a great benefit to them in this matter of car distribution. The car distribution clause in the Manitoba Grain Act has had the effect of increasing the price paid to them by the big elevator men and has redounded to the great benefit of the farmers in the matter of selling their grain. I have letters to show where farmers have taken grain to the elevators ana been offered a certain price for it, and not being satisfied with the price, and having decided to ship the grain to a commission house, rather than have the grain shipped cut the elevator man has come to the rescue and paid the difference in price, that has amounted in some cases to seven or eight cents a bushel. Therefore, the farmers view with a great deal of alarm any interference wdth this clause which permits them to order cars, turn about with the elevators, and in that way get the advantage of shipping their grain to a commission house or wherever they wish to send it. I am very pleased to see the stand which the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) has taken on this question.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mi. Sharpe) two years ago made a memorable speech which was of great benefit in my constitu-

enoy in the last election. I had occasion to use that speech more than once. It showed the breadth of -view of the hon. gentleman who, I am glad to see, retains that same breadth of view, and is not governed by partisan motives in discussing this Bill, viewing the question altogether from the standpoint of his constituency. Everything has been said that can be said for and against this Bill. I want to place myself on record as in favour of the car distribution clauses in the Manitoba Grain Act being left as they are.

I have no fault to find with the discussion on this section. I do not think it has been a partisan discussion; it has been a discussion of men with different views, looking at it from different standpoints. It may be that as we are all human, some of us have the fear or the desire of our constituents behind us, but after all the discussion has been very fair, based on the view of each individual member, as to how it would affect the whole. I want to find a little fault with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I think it would have been just as well if he had not given a little support to the theory that there is an irrepressible and persistent conflict between farmers and railroads. It is not necessary that it should be so.
I have scriptural authority for the position that there is always a difference of opinion between the buyer and the seller.

I am not finding fault with the hon. gentleman for holding his opinion. Anything which tends to accentuate and pernetuate the idea _ that two great sections of the community shall and' must be eternally in conflict with each other, is not in line with the principles of human progress. There may be differences between them, but we ail feel that as we get to know each other better wars will cease. After all, broadly speaking, is not the interest of the railways of that great western country absolutely bound up with the prosperity of the farmer, and is not the best interest of the farmer absolutely bound up with his relations to the great transport interests?
If the relations are properly adjusted, yes.

any other question I am not prepared to say.
Now, the Grain Growers' Association are militant; they are on the watch. The very moment this Credit Men's Association petition was scattered through the country, their notices went out. Here is something that is going to rob us of our car distribution clauses; that we must not allow; be active and be alive, and flood your members and the ministers with petitions against it. But does that prove to you or to me that the farmers would object, if they knew just what was proposed and the spirit in which it was proposed- that it was not by a lot of men caballing against their interests, but by legislators using the best opportunities they had for information, and doing what they considered best in the premises to alleviate slightly the conditions of congestion and hardship, when those conditions arose, and when after examination they proved them to be conditions which ought to be alleviated? If we could sit down alongside of each one of them and tell them exactly what it was proposed and meant to do, does anybody believe that the farmers of the Northwest would be dead against making any letter or syllable or word of alteration in these car clauses? I do not think so. Now, I have approached this question as_ a novice and a tyro, knowing almost nothing about it; but I have given some hard work and close attention to it, and to my^ mind it is a most interesting and absorbing question. I do not look on tnis as a matter which is before us now and may pass away in a few weeks or a few months. I look on this questioin of grain production and grain carriage in our vast Northwest, only the fringes of which have Been developed so far, as one of the most absorbing, one of the most important, and one of the most vital questions we have to deal with in this parliament, and one upon which very great interests in this country are dependent. I have approached this question without the least idea of party interest or party advantage, i want to see the best solution for the best outcome of that great problem, and it will take us this year and several years after this, if we put our whole purpose and our whole effort to it, to have it practically arid finally and satisfactorily solved. This little clause which I am introducing is not a violation of legislation which exists in the Manitoba Grain Act, nor a violation of legislation which we have adopted in this parliament this year. It is simply a further application of a discretion by a responsible body which is upon the scene of action, which knows and ought to know-and if it does not know it will not be doing its duty as a commission-the ins and outs of the whole business in that great Northwest-a dis-Mir. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
cretion by which, when a call comes from a lamed section, from a hurt portion, from a diseased'part of that great organism in the Northwest, they will be able in some little measure to apply the humanitarian principle, and send help sharply and quickly, even though some in better positions have to be delayed for a little time in the beginning. If a man is drowning in the river every other man who has the heart and soul of a. man in him is willing to go to the help of the man who is in trouble, even though it takes from him hours of his good time, and robs him of some of his profits. It is humanitarian. When this matter came up, and those five delegates, who you say represented the united farmers of the west, were in my office, and I put to them the proposition: here is damp grain, liable to damage and utter loss, held to the amount of ten or twelve or fifteen million bushels, by less fortunate men than you, who got your crops, or some of them out, and that is a call, I think, upon our humanity; not a. man of them offered a word against it, but every man of them said: Yes, there will be no objection among the farmers to that; it is only common humanity. That arises from the fact that you are close to them, and you can tell them just what you mean to do, and they can sit down and talk it over with you. I think the case was well put when it was said: if you can relieve the district where want and distress are imminent without much disorganizing the general plan for the healthy sections, is it not in the interest of the farmers of the v'hole country that you should have some power to do it? Some one makes the suggestion, let the Governor in Council do that. Great goodness! the Governor in Council sitting here in Ottawa, consisting of fifteen laymen, perhaps half of them distributed over this country at any given time, knowing absolutely nothing about railways grain transport, with the exception of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, and some others of us, who have travelled on passes in private cars, but having no grasp at all on the situation in the Northwest, stretching from the lakes to the rocky mountains. How can they do it? There is nobody that can do it sympathetically and well, and with a knowledge of the circumstances, but the three men who are devoted to that, who are the priests that minister at the altars of the great grain business in the Northwest, and who know just what is necessary for healing and for comfort. Now, that is all that this provision does; wrhy should we object to it? Why should we suppose that these men are going to run amuck? Why should we suppose that they will throw everything into confusion? It will not be to their interest to do it; it

will not be in accordance with their sympathies to do it; it will not be in accordance with the spirit of the Grain Act to do it. Their discretions are to be nsed within the purposes and lines of the Grain Act itself, and the Grain Act, if it means anything, means the relief of congestion and the quick despatch of grain. Whenever congestion is relieved and grain is made to travel quickly, that is for the benefit of the farmer behind, who has more grain to take the place of that which is moved out, and which is waiting, and anxiously waiting for the time when that will be moved out. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), laid much stress on this, and he is right to a certain extent, that the commission, after due _ examination, and finding that, in their judgment, it is advisable and necessary that the call for help in some parts shall be heeded at cnee, when they do that, may draw away from the general distribution some cars that are necessary to relieve that congested part. So they may to a certain extent.
But they certainly have this power as well:	They have the power and the right
to go to the railway companies and say:
'We want some extra cars put in there,' and they may get them. But suppose the railway company turns on them and says: * We have no extra cars. All our cars are filling in the programme to hundreds of stations and hundreds of districts all over that Northwest, each man having his car ordered, each elevator has a car order, we are filling in all those with every car that we have.' .Well, then if you have no more extra cars draw away a little portion from every one of those places and help the portion which is in dire distress. You will do the least possible harm to the others and you will do the greater possible good to those that are in distress. My heart is no more soft than the hearts of other members around this table, but I have letters in my office which would almost make a man's heart bleed. I have one letter in my office of a man living out some 18 miles from his station, a newcomer who was in debt for everything that he had been using, and his implements as well, who had got his grain at last harvested and threshed out lately but who had no order in for a car that could possibly get to him for months may be in the state of shortage and congestion there. Teaming in with his two teams a portion of his grain, what did he find? He had no cars. The car track buyer was there, but there was no car that the track buyer had into which he could put this man's grain if he had bought it. The man on the street was there, or thereabouts, but the man on the street could not buy his grain. He had no place to put it if he bought it;
the elevator was chuck full and had not been emptied for a long time. That man tried in vain to sell his grain or to store it, but there was no storing place for it. He took his grain back to his own farm again and kept it there. Others piled their grain out behind somebody's shed and covered it over, may be with some straw; they cannot sell it. Now it does seem to me that talk as we like about elevators and about our corporations, that if that elevator could have been emptied of its
50,000	or 60,000 bushels of grain there would have been a chance for that man with his wagonloads of grain to have sold it, because there would have been a place to store it if it had been sold. It seems to me that taking all these things into consideration it is not so serious a matter we are discussing that it will break up the whole car order system, and that if you do this you might as well burn the Grain Act. These assertions do not tally with the facts, and it seems to me that, looking at it from the point of view of those who are trying to do the best they can for that great interest, we have got to use our own judgment, getting at the view of the people interested as far as we can, and by using that judgment in this way, and giving this discretion to the Board of Commissioners, we are putting a piece of machinery there for use in individual cases of hardship involving sometimes total loss which means very much to those who have to bear that loss; we are putting a piece of machinery there which will enable a live and competent man to relieve distress, to aid in the despatch of grain and so to lighten the whole position. I would read something from a letter addressed to me by Mr. Fream, in order to show the way in which he approaches this matter.
It has been rumored that section 207 of the Grain Bill will be considerably changed. This section is, we consider, one of the most important in the Act and one on which considerable time and attention should be bestowed before allowing any changes to be made.
That is Mr. Frcam's position. That is a reasonable position. That is what we have been doing here, bestowing time and attention upon this Act because of its importance, and before making any change in it He goes on to say:
It gives a privilege to the farmer which is his only safeguard against the elevator interests, and while a determined onslaught has repeatedly been made upon this provision yet the opponents of same have never yet been able to present any logical argument why a change should be made. Before this clause was added to the Grain Act the farmers were completely at the mercy of the | interests, and if the clause is removed



We none of us think of removing it.
or in any way weakened by dangerous amendments which might be made to give two different meanings

We are not weakening it, we are strengthening it. We are not putting dangerous amendments there which might have two different meanings. We are putting a plain definite amendment, as plain as the English language can make it, and for purposes which are clearly to be understood. If that is done, he goes on to say:
Conditions will he such that in a short time the farmers would find the car distribution and the general treatment they would receive from the railway companies and the elevator interests even more intolerable than they were before the clause was introduced into the Act.
I would be disposed to agree with Mr. Fream as to the probable results providing things were done to weaken the clauses, or amendments were placed there that were dangerous, or had a double meaning, or if the purpose of these amendments were to do away with the efficacy of the Grain Act in its distribution clauses. To my mind it is to strengthen those rather than to weaken them. If I thought the clause Would weaken them I would drop it at once. Believing that it would strengthen them and would be worked out to the good of the transportation of the farmers' grain in the west, I submit it to the committee and ask for its passage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although there has been a good deal said on this question by western members who object, as I do myself, to any changes being made in this clause, there is one point that I do not think has been brought out, although it is one that the farmers of the west most strongly object to. It is the question of prices.. As a great many of the members from the west know, in a great many places-certainly in the case of the majority of towns along the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern where there is only one elevator. Now, we have found from experience that when a farmer brings his grain to the elevator there is no competition whatever. He looks at the market quotations at Winnipeg and finds possibly that oats are 35 cents a bushel here, but the local elevator only offers him 20 cents. He knows the cost of transportation, which is a matter of about eight cents, and if he finds he can make three or four cents a bushel on his grain he orders a car and ships that grain to Winnipeg. Now, if you make a change whereby the farmer is not able to do that, if you deprive him Oj the privilege of disposing of his grain outside he is compelled to sell to the local elevators at whatever price the elevator Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
operator demands. In my own section of the country that is the objection which has been taken to making any change in this clause, rather than on the car question. I know where a certain price was offered for grain at an elevator, but the farmer was not satisfied, and knowing the Winnipeg price he loaded a car, and the same elevator man offered him 12 cents more for the grain so loaded. That is why the farmers are so much alarmed about the proposed change. It is not a question of cars or car shortage, but simply that they fear the change will place them in the hands of their own local dealer. They cannot draw the grain to the next elevator, which is probably 10 or 15 miles away, they simply have to sell to him if this clause goes through.
So, you place the farmer at once at the .mercy of the local dealer; and I think that is the reason the farmers are objecting so much. I have known small farmers not having enough grain to make a carload, and two of them clubbing together to ship a car. I am very much opposed to the proposed change. In Alberta and the far west, there is no doubt about it, if this change is made, the farmers will have to take whatever price is offered by the local elevator where there is no competition; and even where there are two or three, they will combine and pay only a certain price. And the farmer will make five or six or even ten cents a bushel in loading cars for the Winnipeg market.

I would like to make my position perfectly clear in this matter. This amendment covers the whole of clause 207 of the Bill. There are five subsections in the amendment. The first, (a), is in connection with an elevator collapsing; (b), is in connection with the relief of damp grain; (c), is in connection with seed grain (d), is in connection with heating grain. All these I favour. But subsection (e), in my humble opinion, goes a little too far. I would not give that power to the commission. If I were voting on this section separately, I would certainly vote against the insertion of this subsection (e), of the amendment. If I have to vote on the whole five at once, I will have to vote for the amendment.
The natural way is to take it clause by clause.

If it is taken clause by clause I will vote for the first four and against the fifth. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Roster) has brought to the attention of the committee the conditions in western Canada in connection with the grain blockade. We all know the conditions there. I had a letter the other day from a man who went from my part of the constituency in the province of Manitoba, who tells me that he draws

his grain to the elevator, a distance of forty miles, and then must bribe the elevator people to take the grain off his hands before they will take it. I say these conditions should not be allowed to exist. But this Grain Bill does not cover these conditions. We are allowing the railway companies to build branch line after branch line, and that is the reason, largely, for the congestion. The hopper is too large for the spout. We have to get a new outlet for the grain.
Hear, hear.
To the south.
No, not to the south not by a long way. My hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Douglas), said that my speech of two years ago did him a lot of good in his campaign
I also found it very helpful.

You did not use it fairly then. I stand by that speech just as on the day I made it. And I stood by it through my campaign, and it was on account of that speech that I was able to win out against my opponent-and I could do it again to-morrow. I simply arose to explain my position in connection with this matter.

I wish to say just a word with regard to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster, North Toronto). It seems to me that in referring to the words of Mr. Fream, who said that the present law on this subject should not be weakened in any way, I understood him to say that it . will not be weakened by this amendment. As I understand the law now, the farmers themselves have the control of placing cars according to the order in which they have been called for. When you givej another body power to do away with the distribution of cars, you are taking away from the farmers the protection they have under the present law. The burden is upon my hon. friend (Mr. Foster, North Toronto), to show that the present law has worked unfairly, that it has caused dissatisfaction, and hardship. Else why make the change? If the law has worked well-and every hon. gentleman I have heard speak on the subject admits that it works fairly well-I do not see why any change should be made. As to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe), I think he can make his mind easy, for we can take a vote upon the different clauses of the amendment. And, feeling as I do, being in accord with my hon. friend, if there is no other way to take the vote, I will move as an amendment to the amendment that subsection (e) be struck out. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will move that himself. If he does,
I shall have much pleasure in seconding it.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but this is perhaps a more important portion of the Bill than the committee has pet appreciated. I should judge from the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he has not yet fully appreciated the importance of the section, or the relationship that must of necessity exist between the farmer on the one hand, and those who buy and transport his grain on the other. It is not throwing any suspicion upon the grain dealer or railway company to say that in the buying and handling of grain their interests are not the interests of the farmers. It is an absolute necessity of the case, just as it is that two and two make four, that the farmer, and the railway company and grain dealers are in opposition to each other, and that opposition is apt to be a very strenuous one.
I do not wish to introduce controversial matter into the discussion, but if my hon. friend is not aware of the facts, it is his misfortune. The fact is that there is necessarily and actually a very bitter feeling and always has been-I do not know what it will be in the future, but it exists today-between the two opposing interests. It is no aspersion upon either of them to say that there is such a feeling, and it is not a proper appreciation of the facts to suggest that by any legislation We can do away with that condition. It is a natural condition, it is not an improper condition, except as it may be strained to improper limits. My hon. friend will be the greatest legislator that ever graced this parliament or any other, if he can bring those two interests into amicable conjunction. I want to impress upon the minister that this matter is one the importance of which cannot be exaggerated, that the action taken tonight is going to have far reaching consequences, and the responsibility thereof must rest upon my hon. friend and his colleagues. I want to allude to the argument made by the minister as to the urgency of the provision of sdbsection (e). He painted a picture of the deplorable loss to be suffered by reason of damp grain; and the necessity of rushing cars to the relief of the locality suffering from that condition. But my hon. friend does not appreciate the fact that subsection (e) has no necessary application to that condition. On the face of it, it applies to the locality and the condition where the grain is abundant, and may be as good as it is abundant. It applies to the condition of congestion, and gives authority to the commission to relieve that congestion. He sketched the condition to which clause (b) would be applicable; but I say that is not the condition that clause (e) is intended to pto-

vide for. From the wording of that clause it applies rather to a condition where the grain is merely abundant, and may be just as good as it is abundant. In such a case the board has the authority of this parliament to suspend the provisions of the Act in regard to car distribution, both at that point where it must go for oars, and at this point to which it will send cars. That is a radical change in the provision regarding car distribution. There can be no misapprehension in regard to the construction to be given those words. The member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) was insistent that it was right and proper to give authority to the board to order cars forward in special cases. There is no special case in subsection (e). Subsection (e) does not provide for a special case, it provides for a general condition. Take the condition that exists in the west to-day, a general condition of congestion, and the board has the right under that section to order any distribution of cars it pleases in any part of the west.
Is not that just what we are driving at, the very thing you have enunciated?
I am glad that my hon. friend appreciates the meaning of the section, but it is not the meaning which we wish to have attached to the legislation.
Does the hon. gentip-man mean that under the authority of this clause a general order could be made to 'lie Tailway companies?
Surely.

1 think the hon. gentleman who sits behind him will tell him that no suoh order could be made. The Supreme Court has ruled over and over again in eases much less decisive that no general order could be made under the authority of that clause. It would have to be an order of cars to a special point.

I am saying that under the condition that exists in the northwest to-day the Grain Commission, under the terms of that order, would have full authority to send oars wherever they pleased and whenever they pleased. To-day, if that section were in force, the provisions in regard to oar order booking would be to all intents and purposes suspended throughout the northwest. Those are the actual facts of the ease. I do not suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce understands it in that way, but I am giving him my understanding of it, with a knowledge of the conditions.
There is another point. As the law stands at present the farmer who has grain to ship knows what his rights! are, he knows what he may expect. But Mr. OLIVER.
if you introduce the provision of clause (e), or even the provision of (b), but especially (e), then the farmer does not know where he stands in regard to his car order. As long as the law stands as it is be gets [DOT]his order in. his .turn with his neighbours, but give the commission the discretion that you are proposing to them there-they take the cars from here and send them there- and he is out of his calculations entirely as the result of this legislation. I do not want to delay the committee, I do not want to hold back tlhe passage of this legislation, but I want to emphasize to the minister that he is dealing with that part of the Bill that is most far-reaching, that touches most closely the people who are most affected by the Bill, and that in my humble judgment, and I give it for what it is worth, this section will not he limited to the degree that he believes it will be, that it will go so fax beyond that limit that it will have the effect, to all intents and purposes, of destroying the value of the oar-distribution provision in the Grain Act as it stands at the present time.
With regard to the provisions in Bill (No. 96) as to forwarding cars for the relief of localities where there is damaged grain, if there were a few isolated localities where the gram was damaged, it would be possible, as it would be right, to provide that this Grain Commission be given authority to specially forward cars to these localities. It was such a condition, no doubt, that the delegates had in mind when they discussed the matter with the minister, but, to-day, with the condition that prevails throughout the prairie provinces, with respect to damaged grain here, there and yonder in a hundred different locali-_ ties, there is no advantage in giving the right to the commission to send cars to one place or to another place. There are not cars enough available, there is no possibility of them meeting the requirements by any orders, they may give, -and it just reduces the matter to the point that they will send the cars wherever the loudest noise is made, or wherever the biggest pull exists, which is a most objectionable condition of affairs. That is a feature of the case that did not strike me at the time the Bill was going through the House, but it is the absolute condition, and it may be just as well to be understood in thalt way.
Is not that the condition prevailing in railway circles in Ontario now?

I could not say, I am sure; but that is the condition that prevails in the west. The condition of damage is so widespread, that there is no possibility of meeting that condition by any special orders that might be given and to

give authority to issue special orders under such conditions is simply to give authority to abrogate the advantages of the Bill for the man who wants to use those advantages. We have given the privilege of loading platforms to the farmers in the west. They tried to get them for a long time. They were successful in getting them at last. They have handled a large part of their grain over these loading platforms. Those loading platforms are a cause of offence to the elevator man, to the local grain dealer, and to the railway company, and there is no doubt that: do away with the car distribution clause and the loading platforms might just as well disappear from the scene.
The question has been asked: Who are the men who are demanding changes in this Act, with regard to car distribution? There was some question about it put forward. There is no question about it. Three years ago, when the Grain Act was under amendment, notice was sent by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce to all parties interested, to come and be heard, in regard to these amendments. The matter was public, everybody was admitted and we found there the railway man, the grain dealer, the one side, even the banker, lined up on the one side, every one of them demanding the abrogation of the section of the Act relating to car distribution, and the farmer on the other. There is no secret about who is on the one side, and who is on the other. There is no blame to either party, because they are on the respective ' sides, but there never has been any mistake about it, or misunderstanding that on the one side is the producer, and on the other are the interests that necessarily 'handle his product. There is just the same necessary conflict of interest between these two sections of the community as there was between the buyer and the seller in the days of King Solomon, and has been every day since.

I would like to ask the minister whether he proposes having a vote taken upon each clause? The reason I ask it is that members of the committee might not entertain the same view of this clause as they do of others. I think there is quite a cousensus of opinion in favour of the other clauses, but there is a very strong objection to clause (e). That objection has been expressed very strongly on this side of the House, end if my hon. friend will not allow the vote to be taken on the different clauses, I would move that-the proposed new section be amended by striking out clause (e).

I have no objection to taking them paragraph by paragraph.
Subsection (b) agreed to on division.
Subsection (e) agreed to, yeas 44, nays 29.
I did not vote because I am paired with the member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler).

I did not vote because I am paired with Mr. Foster.
On section 208-inspection divisions.

The object of the amendment to section 208 is to perfect the erection of Calgary into an inspection division. It follows the provisions with respect to Winnipeg making such changes as are necessary to apply similar conditions to Calgary.

On the 3rd reading I shall move an amendment to section 246.
On section 13-acquiring of terminal elevators.

Do I understand that this section would allow the board to declare that elevators not only upon the Great Lakes, at Fort William and Port Arthur, but also upon the eastern side of the lakes and at Atlantic ports, terminal elevators, that these elevators being so declared the government has power to either construct elevators or to take over existing elevators? I am not able to see why the provision should not be general, why elevators might not be taken over and operated by the government to as much advantage on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and on the St. Lawrence as at Fort William and Port Arthur.

This gives power to the Governor in Council to construct, acquire, lease or expropriate any terminal elevator, if parliament has granted the money for such purpose; and a terminal elevator is an elevator which exists at what has been declared by the board to be a terminal point. The only terminal point at the present time is Fort William and Port Arthur.

I do not see why that should be so. I do not see why the board should have the power to limit and fix what shall be terminal points. Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, St. John, Tiffin, Port McNichol, Vancouver and Victoria, are just as much terminal points as Port Arthur and Fort William. It may be that in connection with the administration of the Grain Act the board might very well be given the power to declare a certain point to be a terminal point; but why this board should have the power to say in effect that the government may construct or take over an elevator at Fort William and Port Arthur, but shall have no right to construct or take over an elevator at any other point which, in reality, is just

as much a terminal point as Fort William or Port Arthur, I fail to understand. I would suggest to my hon. friend whether or not this provision might not well be broadened out. The grain does not stop at Fort William and Port Arthur. It moves forward to the Atlantic ports, and on to the English markets, and there is just as much, or almost as much, reason for the government owning and controlling elevators at Atlantic ports and also at the eastern ports on the Great Lakes as at Port Arthur and Fort William. But what I do decidedly object to is that this board shall have the power to decide at what points the government shall take over or construct elevators, and own and manage them.

Certainly, the board should not have that power. It has not the power to establish inspection divisions, except with the approval of the Governor in Council, and it ought not to have the still greater power of saying which should be a terminal point, without the approval of the Governor in Council.
Therefore, I move that subsection (y) of section 2 be amended by striking out tlie word ' board ' and substituting therefor the words ' Governor in Council.'
Amendment agreed to.

The idea that the hon. member for St. John has in mind would be met if the word ' public ' were inserted either before or after the word ' terminal ' in section 13. That would be an elevator that actually did all the work of a terminal elevator, but had not the standing of a terminal elevator for the purpose of issuing warehouse receipts; that is, to do in the eastern terminal elevators just what the hon. member for St. John had in mind.
I do not propose to widen it in that way.

I think we ought to discuss the whole question of elevators under section 13. Speaking for the port of St. John, there is the most urgent necessity for additional elevator accommodation for the shipment of grain at that port.
The elevator at St. John was constructed by the Canadian Pacific Company, with some assistance from the city, and the provincial government. It was large enough when it was built, and for some years afterwards, but the business has developed so rapidly, that that elevator is wholly incapable of accommodating the business, and the result is there is great congestion. During the present year the business to that port has already very considerably exceeded the business of last year which was very large indeed. Last year I think the exports from St. John Mr. PUGSLEY.
reached the very handsome total of about $25,000,000, and up to the present time they are about $2,000,000 ahead of what they were last year. It seems to me that when we are considering the question of giving the government authority to either expropriate existing elevators or to build new ones, we ought to have some statement from the government as to what is their intention. I have no doubt myself that we have been altogether lacking in the past in the matter of making sufficient provision in the way of elevator accommodation east of the Great Lakes. It is true that during recent years great additional elevator accommodation has been provided at Tiffin and Victoria Harbour. In that respect both the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk railways are doing their duty. There is, however, only accommodation for a few million bushels east of the Great Lakes, while in the city of Buffalo there is elevator accommodation for pretty well on to 50,000,000 bushels which is far and away ahead of anything we have in Canada. By reason of this enormous accommodation, vast quantities of Canadian grain go to Buffalo which ought to be carried to Canadian ports east of the Great Lakes, and the business of transporting that grain is lost to Canada. It seems to me the government must increase the accomodation upon the eastern shores of the Great Lakes, upon the St. Lawrence and upon our Atlantic seaboard. No doubt the same remark will apply to the Pacific coast.
Where does the grain come from that reaches St. John by rail?
Some by all rail. Some comes, strange to say, from the American west, although we get more package freight for them.
It only gets to St. John by rail.

Yes. At the present time the Canadian Pacific is bringing a good deal of grain by the all rail route north of lake Superior. There is this curious fact in connection with the trade of St. John, that while our whole export trade up to the present time exceeds that of last year by more than $2,000,000, that increase is almost entirely in American products. The increase of Canadian products carried to the port has only amounted to two or three hundred thousand dollars, while the increase in American products amounts to very nearly $2,000,000. I think the total Canadian products carried to St. John have amounted up to the present time to something over $7,000,000, and the total of American products between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000.

My hon. friend has given us some interesting information with reference to the increase in the trade of the port of St. John which we are all glad to know. But I think he is mixing up two different things. The Dominion parliament and the Dominion government have the right to build elevators in St. John now if they choose to. The purposes of this Act are special purposes looking to the regulation of the grain trade from the west, and specially at the great terminal points. Certain abuses have existed and it was contended that the control and supervision of the government at those points was not sufficient to protect the grain shippers and the grain exporters and the clause under discussion is meant to in some way cope with that difficulty.
By the government acquiring the elevators?
That is the principle involved in clause 13. We take the power to lease or construct.
Is it intended to do it?
Yes. There will be a grant of money asked for during the present session for the purpose of doing it, but I am not in a position to say how large the amount of money will be.

I agree to a great extent with the hon. member for St. John as to the desirability of including in this policy the eastern elevators as well as those in the west. It would be quite easy to include within the scope of the Bill these eastern terminal elevators. The capacity of those at Midland and Port McNicoll only amounts to about 5,000,000 bushels, but elevators now are being built on a new principle. The Grand Trunk elevator at Midland and that of the Canadian Pacific at Port McNicoll are to-day so well equipped that it simply means the addition of more tanks to increase the capacity from one and a quarter to two and a half million bushels; and I am told some of them might be increased beyond that. It is simply a question of motive power. If the government can see their way to do this to embrace in the Bill the eastern elevators it would be most desirable and I hope the minister will be able to make the necessary provision in this Bill.

The proviso is in the Bill and the powers are given, in the definition of ' Terminal Elevator ' as my hon. friend will see:
' Terminal elevator ' includes every elevator or warehouse which receives or ehips grain, and is located at any point declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal point.
This links up with section 13, under which the Governor in Council has power
to-
-construct, acquire, lease or expropriate for His Majesty any terminal elevator if parliament has granted the money for such purpose.
So all powers needed are contained in the Bill. I do not wish it to be understood that the government is proposing to undertake the building of all the elevators east and west. It certainly is not proposing to do anything of the kind. And, for the present, it has no plans to construct, lease and operate terminal elevators at any other place than Fort William. The time may come when that policy will be extended to Prince Rupert, Vancouver or some other point on the Pacific, to Hudson Bay or to other places which the Governor in Council, after due consideration, deems it necessary to control in this way. But I do not want the committee to think for a moment that the government proposes to take in charge the building of these elevators. Something is to be left to private and corporate activity, and I think a great deal must be left to that in the future.
If I may be allowed a question, is it not because of the fact that it has been left to private and corporate enterprise at Fort William and Port Arthur that difficulty has arisen?
There are great difficulties between a point like Fort William and Port Arthur and many of the other points mentioned, as the hon. gentleman will see if he thinks of it for a moment.	.
In what respect?

The head of the Lakes is the point at which nearly all the grain that passes out centres within a small radius and passes through, and it is there that the particular difficulties are to be met with of which complaint has been made.
Aire not Halifax and St. John two points at which all the grain concentrates that goes to Europe ?
No, it does not all go through Halifax and St. John.
In the winter season ?

No. As a matter of fact, the same causes of difficulty that have operated and led to dissatisfaction at Fort William and Port Arthur have not operated and have not been complained of in the eastern elevators.

These elevators iare under supervision and will be kept under supervision, and, as is necessary, they will be kept under stricter and stricter supervision. But at the present time there is no grievance, no cause why these should be taken up 'all of a sudden and put in the same position as the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. A certain amount of grain goes out through St. John, -and I hope that in future more of it wild go out that way. Precautions have been taken which, in the course of the trade, I think, have allowed to rise only one or two oases in which a grievance has existed in shipping grain from Halifax or St. John. Grain is shipped from Montreal, and the elevators there iare under supervision in the same way. The supervision and power of the government follows the grain from Winnipeg to all these different places to the time of its transhipment 'across the ocean. These elevators are carefully looked after, and, if it becomes necessary, as the traffic increases, that they be more carefully looked after, iamd supervision added to and strengthened, it will be the duty of the government, as it was the purpose of the government, to see that this is done.
Do I understand the minister to say that he will 'be prepared to make a statement at some stage of the Bill in regard to the government ownership of terminals?

I have made a pretty full statement; but if that does not satisfy my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), when we come to some other portion of the Bill that matter can be taken up and he can put the questions which he thinks are necessary.
In the lack of fuller information, it will be necessary, on the third reading to move the amendment of this section.
I think we have had a pretty good siege of it today. I would like to have finished the thing, as leaving it over means that it will probably take an hour or two longer.
Can the minister say without inconvenience, what sections of the Bill still stand?

Yes, sections 3, 121, 122, 124 and 125. These are the sections that remain, and there may be another section to be added.
Progress reported.
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto) moved the adjournment of the House.

Mr. Speaker, before the House adjourns I would like to make a statement. My attention has been called to the fact that at first sight there appears to be a slight contradiction between one part of my speech delivered in this House on the 22nd. of January last and another part of my remarks. In looking into the question, I see that something has been omitted and I wish to have the matter put right. I wish to state that on page 1,695 of ' Hansard,' line 9, after the words ' and religious point of view ' the following should be inserted:
' This is the condition of affairs which existed before the 2nd April, 1908. The Ne Temere decree now forbids, from a Catholic religious point of view only, mixed marriages before a non-Catholic clergyman,, but this is a matter which affects only Catholics and their conscience. It has no civil effect and does not affect those who are non-Catholics. As the ' Tablet ' puts it, the Catholic church has no power to change the civil law of marriage. The impediments to marriage which were in force on the first of August, 1866, continue to exist, but those created after do not come under article 125 of our Civil Code which speaks only of impediments hitherto existing.'
What business will be taken up on Thursday?

After the softening influences of Ash Wednesday have been experienced by us all, I think it is the intention to take up the Post Office Bill and probably the Tariff Commission Bill, and to give a step forward to the Manitoba Boundaries Bill.
